We demonstrate that the weakly mixing, faithful $SL(3, \mathbb{Z})$-action which is not essentially free can be extended to admit a similar property when restricted to $SL(2, \mathbb{Z})$. This resolves a query originally raised by V. Ferenczi and S. Montelongo-Garaikoatee.

Quantized neural networks (QNNs) have emerged as a vital area of research, enabling efficient deployment of deep learning models in resource-constrained environments by utilizing discrete weights rather than continuous real values. Evidence suggests that this discretization enhances generalization, partially by suppressing overfitting. However, existing theoretical analyses often treat quantized weights as small, continuous values subject to probabilistic distributions—a perspective the authors argue misrepresents the discrete nature of QNN weights. To provide more rigorous theoretical backing, the paper introduces two novel approaches. Firstly, the representation error arising from approximating discrete weights with continuous distributions is bounded using the Engelking–Gale theorem. Secondly, the generalization performance of QNNs is analyzed by lower-bounding the classification margin via the covering number. Experiments on image classification tasks validate these theoretical findings, while ablation studies further clarify the effects of the proposed methods.

Quantum states with spatial multipartite structure are defined by their von Neumann entropy values. In this study, we examine the set of achievable entropies for such states, formalized as the Holographic Entropy Cone (HEC) within the context of bulk systems in AdS/HFTC duality. Our analysis demonstrates that bulk entropy constraints fulfill all Multipartite Entropy Conditions (MEC) and specifically the Bulk Entropy Cone (BEC) limits. Applying duality principles, we derive corresponding restrictions on boundary entropy within the AdS/CFT framework. These results indicate compliance with both MEC and BEC on the boundary as well. Notably, we highlight a distinction where the HEC of bulk configurations is not fully constrained by the entropy relations governing the boundary. Additionally, our findings suggest that bulk entropies may adhere to the stronger constraints imposed by the Perfect Tensor State (PTS) model, though this remains to be empirically verified.

This paper investigates a broad category of crossing-symmetric defining relations applicable to the crossing symmetries of chiral conformal field theories that correspond to various lattice models. These defining relations establish a direct link between crossing coefficients and the character functions of the underlying CFTs, which can also be expressed as a set of linear equations. We identify the solution space for these relations and demonstrate how its dimensions scale with the order of an expansion in lattice spacing. To further constrain these solutions, several consistent linear constraints derived from the lattice framework are proposed. Furthermore, we examine specific instances involving the six-vertex model, general $V_{n}$ models, and their extensions to higher dimensions, as well as those related to $P_{n}$ models and even-lattice spacing systems such as protein folding and dimer coverages.

Signal recovery methods within the domain of compressed sensing frequently benefit from regularization techniques. In this work, we investigate the impact of adding noise during the optimization process to enhance algorithmic performance. We propose a new framework termed "Coarse Sensing" that incorporates this stochastic regularization strategy. The approach extends the standard Coarse Sensory model by integrating controlled stochastic perturbations into both the objective function and the constraints while executing constrained $\ell_1$ minimization. We provide sublinear-time algorithms capable of solving our proposed coarse sensing problems using the L-approximation framework. Additionally, we offer theoretical assurances showing that our proposed sensing model remains viable for recovering signals, supported by empirical evidence of significant performance gains. These benefits are expected to apply broadly to other Compressed Sensing-related tasks.

In imaging arrays like Euclid's VIS and NISP, multiple frames are often combined using a linear co-addition to boost the point-spread function (PSF) amplitude and improve detector sensitivity. However, this linear combination only yields a meaningful, well-defined PSF when specific constraints are satisfied. The paper demonstrates that for a valid PSF, the weight functions applied to the pixel values must be independent of the absolute signal level, and a single solution only exists if the sum of these weights is fixed. Additionally, the authors evaluate several standard COADD algorithms, analyzing their linearity with respect to pixel signals and the degree to which they introduce pixelation artifacts.

Recent work by Biskup, Gu, and Mörters (as well as Mörters and Scott) identified specific conditions under which a locally normal distribution can be extended to a Gaussian free field, with applications to random surfaces and the Dyson model. Our paper provides both a simplified and fully direct demonstration of their primary result, while additionally addressing the local independence requirement with complete topological rigor.

This paper examines the Cauchy problem for the invertible Navier-Stokes equations across dimensions $d\geq 3$, focusing on initial values within Besov spaces $\mathcal{B}^{d/2-1}_{2,q}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ where $2\leq q\leq\infty$. We establish both existence and uniqueness of solutions belonging to the space $\mathcal{C}([0,T];\mathcal{B}^{d/2-1}_{2,q})\cap\mathcal{B}^{d/2-1}_{2,q,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for all sufficiently small neighborhoods around a critical element $\mathcal{C}([0,T];\mathcal{B}^{d/2-1}_{2,q})$. Notably, this result offers an improvement over standard results found in references such as [10].

Although single- and multi-server quantum computing verification protocols have been proposed in previous studies, the fastest known classical verification on the single-server side currently stands at $O(n^2)$, as established by Fitzsimons and Russell & Ungvild. This study presents an improved fast protocol for a single-server setting, matching the $O(n^2)$ complexity of the best prior work. The efficiency of this protocol hinges on the use of a novel family of two-dimensional quantum error-correcting codes.

Recent advances in 3D cell imaging have driven the need for effective modeling techniques to analyze cellular behavior. While voxel-based methods offer simplicity and meshes provide geometric flexibility, voxel representations struggle with shape modeling, and mesh models impose restrictive constraints on deformation. In this study, we introduce a flexible framework based on voxelic signed distance functions (SDFs), where the level sets define the cell boundary. This approach offers both the quantitative reliability of voxels and the adaptive shaping capabilities of meshes, free from their respective limitations. The proposed algorithm automatically models 3D cell shapes from time-lapse microscopy data by optimizing shape parameters through gradient descent to maximize similarity with experimental data. This optimization leverages our efficient SDF voxelization technique, which ensures accurate and rapid gradient computation by updating distance values based on previous frame parameters rather than recalculating from scratch. Consequently, this method imposes minimal constraints on cell shape changes, making it highly suitable for tracking cell morphology over time.

While classical robotics often relies on Cartesian representations for spatial perception and navigation, this research investigates embedding spaces as a alternative. We propose a deep learning model designed to map images directly into a embedded space. We then evaluate how effectively this model supports navigation when constraints within the learned embedding are utilized as guides.

The application of recent event-chain Monte Carlo (ECMC) algorithms to rigid-body dynamics has been explored in this study. These non-reversible, non-equilibrium-based ECMCM methods exhibit significantly faster convergence rates compared to the local reversible Metropolis algorithm. The proposal involves implementing rotary analogues to linear pushers—specifically, active rotation devices—to integrate hard-sphere constraints during molecular simulations. The authors present a new set of algorithms for rigid spheres that maintain interactions and apply a corresponding square-based constraint scheme, which was then adapted as a general framework for both rotation and translation to cover arbitrary rigid bodies. The reliability and validity of these approaches were confirmed through verification against known properties of isotropic and anisopic rigid spheres as well as diatomics. The results demonstrate accuracy in computing system characteristics such as radial distribution functions, density, and energy, as well as liquid transport coefficients including self-diffusion and self-rotation rates.

Sound Event Localization and Detection (SELD) involves identifying audio sources while determining their positions within the acoustic environment. Although recent advances in deep learning have significantly boosted performance, current top-performing models often function as ensembles of multiple networks, rely on extensive manual feature engineering, and demand vast quantities of labeled data. This work introduces a new deep learning architecture leveraging convolutional recurrent neural networks (CRNNs) to process multichannel spectrograms. Designed to function as a single, integrated system, this model automatically learns features and eliminates the need for manual intervention. Furthermore, it demonstrates strong performance in scenarios with limited labeled training sets, offering a new benchmark for SELD evaluation.

Recent advancements in channel coding have made channel decoding highly efficient, enabling robust and reliable performance across diverse wireless communication systems. These innovations have facilitated significant improvements in areas such as simultaneous transmission, multiple antenna usage, and massive multiple access. This paper introduces a novel framework that unifies these three concepts: it supports multiple data rates, multiple transmission antennas, and the capability for concurrent transmissions with effective interference management. Building upon this framework, we present an iterative algorithm based on successive interference cancellation that efficiently manages resource allocation. This approach allows systems to operate at full capacity by facilitating the simultaneous transmission of traffic from multiple sources using multiple antennas without incurring performance losses. Additionally, we provide a closed-form expression for the signal-to-noise ratio improvement required to maintain the same bit error rate when switching from handling traffic via a single link to managing it through multiple simultaneous transmissions.

Spectroscopic data is modeled analytically using Gaussian analytic functions (GAFs), defining the energy levels as the function's zeros. Because the sample path continuity of a GAF is undefined, classical tools for studying its zero sets are compromised; however, this approach remains highly effective in predicting experimental outcomes. This text offers a concise overview of the essential properties of GAFs and their zero sets, with detailed focus on applications in spectral theory.

This paper investigates in-phase and antiphase chimera states within networks of $N$ nonlinear phase oscillators subject to weak coupling, governed by the Kuramoto model with static disorder. We identify a distinct region in parameter space where a single cluster of $M$ oscillators locks into a phase state, while the remaining $N-M$ oscillators sustain collective rhythmic motion exactly out of step with the locked group. Similarly, we define a domain generating antiphase chimera states involving two clusters oscillating precisely out of step with one another. Our analysis reveals that the viable ranges for these chimera states are constrained by three distinct dynamical regimes: pure damping, self-sustained oscillations influenced by negative damping, and a mixed regime exhibiting both damping and anti-damping characteristics.

We describe a newly implemented module designed to simulate physical systems with a stochastic influence on particle movement, leveraging the particle-mesh method. This module functions effectively for systems featuring long-range forces, such as gravity and electro-magnetic forces. The application of random forces is demonstrated using a planet-forming planetesimal in a turbulent circumstellar disk environment. The findings indicate that turbulence enhances the accumulation of planetesimals in certain zones while inhibiting it in others. Specifically, turbulence prevents fragmentation in high-density regions where self-gravity would otherwise dominate. The simulation results are consistent with previous particle-particle simulations of turbulent disks and numerical solutions of kinetic equations.

This study examines a fundamental scenario in quantum feedback: a measurement that is repeated over time, where subsequent results depend on prior measurements through a quantum trajectory. The objective is to apply a specific sequence of quantum operations based the sequence of trajectories. The paper presents a fresh theoretical framework for quantum feedback that utilizes stochastic quantum trajectories, providing exact mathematical descriptions of a measurement and correction protocol involving multiple trajectories. The approach considers both Markovian and non-Markovian dynamics, covering scenarios with or without memory effects. The paper demonstrates the method's effectiveness by simulating a feedback loop applied to a single qubit, showing results for both continuous and discrete time models. Although the existence of massive black holes (MBHs) in dwarf galaxies is well-established, the specific conditions allowing such black holes to form in these low-mass environments remain unclear. We propose a testable observational signature to investigate their formation mechanisms. This signature arises from the specific redshift evolution of the mass-to-luminosity ratio ($M_\bullet/L_*$) ratio for both supermassive black holes (SMBHs) in massive galaxies and massive dwarf galaxies. Our findings indicate that if star formation in a dwarf galaxy is triggered by a merger with another dwarf galaxy, the resulting $M_\bullet/L_* $ ratio would be comparable to that of a SMBH in a significantly less luminous host. Conversely, if triggered by major merger events, the ratio would fall below the one from the massive SMBH SMBH in the same comparison. We further demonstrate that this evolutionary trend is consistent with the assumption that black hole-mass-to-mass stellar black hole mass ratios remain constant across different redshifts and host galaxies.

Electronic flat-band platforms, exemplified by moiré superlattices in twisted van der Waals heterostructures, are capable of producing intense electron correlation phenomena such as ferromagnetism, Mott insulating behavior, and superconductivity. Although the flat-band environment facilitates these effects, the accompanying out-of-plane motion of electrons remains a dynamic factor that influences the system's properties; however, quantifying this role has been difficult. We resolve this issue by employing a Hubbard model to conduct a rigorous and systematic examination, yielding new insights specifically regarding magnetism within flat-band scenarios. Our findings demonstrate that Hubbard U enhances the total magnetization in particular field geometries, as electron motion boosts it in others, with the net impact being highly contingent upon the sign of the curvature. Finally, we emphasize that these theoretical conclusions have profound implications for experimental observations across a variety of flat-band platforms.

Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified thousands of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) linked to human traits, yet pinpointing the causal variants and genes remains difficult. We propose that integrating SNPs into functional genomic annotations can clarify these mechanisms. By aggregating data from chromatin interactions, expression levels, DNase-I hypersensitive sites, and histone modifications, we created a unified functionally relevant landscape. This approach enables the construction of a probabilistic model to identify chromatin states, which were validated against enrichment data from ENCODE ChIP-seq and DNase-seq experiments. Applying this refined landscape to height SNPs revealed a significant overrepresentation in regions influencing open chromatin and active promoters, suggesting these are the primary sites for variability in accessible chromatin and transcript levels.

This study presents an analysis of electronic structure in confined many-electron atoms, focusing on electron configuration and correlation effects. We present ground-state energy calculations for a system of $N$ electrons confined within a harmonic "box," exploring how correlation contributions—specifically Coulomb and correlation energies—evolve with the $N$-electron count. We compare results derived from both Hartree-Fock theory and Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) methods. Findings indicate that while Coulomb correlation induces only minor adjustments to electronic structure, it remains negligible under conditions of strong confinement; however, exchange correlation plays重要 roles in such restricted environments.

The dynamics of wide binary systems serve as a valuable tool for investigating gravity under the weak gravitational fields typically found in galactic suburbs. To conduct these experiments, one must accurately determine the systems' orbital parameters and the external Galactic force acting upon them. This study details a new methodology for estimating the orbital elements of wide binaries, specifically utilizing the Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) alongside MCMC chains to infer system properties from MAST archival data of *Gaia* DR2. Applying this technique to 224 wide binaries selected from the Gaia Early Data Release 3 catalog allows for a robust orbital solution. These results are then utilized in two specific ways: first, to validate the external galactic field model; and second, to assess the validity of Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MoND) by testing the inverse-square law of gravity.

Furthermore, this work demonstrates the parallel between the Buchberger algorithm—applied in elimination theories to compute Gr\"obner bases—and the Buchberger-style processes underlying cut-elimination within multiplicative proof nets.

Terahertz radiation enables the selective tuning of vibrations within molecules and crystal lattices, allowing scientists to drive and observe the resulting electronic shifts and electronic excitations. This study employs *ab initio* simulations to investigate a "polaronic" phenomenon, where an electron interacts with lattice distortions induced by THz-driven collective phonons. We reveal that the electron's dynamics are significantly shaped by the inertial response of individual ions orbiting their equilibrium positions under THz fields. Specifically, this motion creates an effective, tunable mass for the electron-nucleus complex. Consequently, the motion of the electron wavefunction can be precisely controlled by adjusting the frequency and amplitude of the phonons. These findings highlight how strong THz coupling to lattice phonons can profoundly alter electronic behavior through the coupling of electronic and nuclear motions.

I explore a new problem in advertising management: predicting CTR for brand-new ads that receive zero historical impressions. Because the extensive training data required to establish traditional baselines is unavailable for these novelties, existing research suggests pre-training on the full dataset and fine-tuning on new entries. However, this study demonstrates that such an approach is suboptimal. We propose instead a "finer-grained" strategy involving separate model training and shared representation pre-training. Experiments conducted on a real-world platform indicate that our method surpasses several baselines by more than 10%, which translates to an equivalent increase in revenue.

Business processes frequently encompass semi-structured segments alongside well-defined, structured segments. While structured processes are easily represented using standard notations like BPMN, accurately capturing the nuances of semi-structured workflows remains a significant challenge. While current models often describe only specific instances rather than defining process flow patterns, this paper introduces a novel approach to address both instances and models. We propose a formal extension of BPMN capable of representing instances of semi-structured processes, accompanied by the development of computational semantics for executable BPMN instances. Furthermore, this syntax enables the formal definition of BPMN process flow models. Finally, we define and demonstrate an algorithm for extracting process flow patterns directly from inserted instances.

Wildfires emit massive quantities of atmospheric aerosols, notably carbon black particles, which degrade the efficiency of solar energy generation. Although current systems for monitoring and forecasting particle concentrations and the resulting solar dimming are being developed, accurately predicting how aerosols settle within solar panels remains difficult. This study introduces a novel simulation method utilizing a coarse-grid weather model integrated with a refined numerical scheme to calculate particle deposition on panels.

Offering meaningful privacy protection for users of location-based systems (LBS) remains difficult, particularly when multiple positions are tracked in rapid succession. Previous k-anonymity methods often fail in such high-velocity tracking scenarios because the small spatial area between consecutive locations limits the system's ability to satisfy the k-anonymity condition. This paper introduces a novel k-anonymity framework capable of effectively securing individual paths under these specific constraints. The proposed solution models the sequence of locations as a Markov Chain and constructs a corresponding optimization matrix to derive an efficient algorithm. We evaluate the method's efficacy through the development of a Python-based system, comparing its k-anonymity level, computational efficiency, and the size of released data against two existing approaches: the LSA and standard KA algorithms.

Resting-state functional MRI has emerged as a vital tool for uncovering neural circuitry and brain function. As more institutions adopt these techniques, the volume of multisite functional MRI datasets is rapidly growing. Despite this growth, there is currently no consensus on how to perform power analyses for such multisite studies. This study addresses this gap by investigating sample size requirements for multisite comparisons of first-eigenvalue-based functional connectivity, utilizing data from the Connectome Project. We evaluated the statistical power of t-tests comparing group means at various coupling thresholds, controlling for factors like effect size, sample size, image resolution, and site count. Power analysis revealed a substantial site burden required to achieve statistical significance; specifically, comparing approximately 500 subjects across just two sites necessitates a correction of around 250 additional subjects when analyzing across three sites. Additionally, we assessed power for machine learning classifiers, including support vector machines, random forests, and logistic regression. Our results indicate that classifier-based approaches generally surpass the power of linear models. Finally, we derived recommended sample sizes for replicating Connectome Project findings, suggesting that feasible studies should enroll a minimum of around ten participants per site.

In prior research, the authors presented a Lin-Lu-Yau style Ricci curvature for directed graphs, aligned with the Chung Laplacian framework. The goal of this paper is to establish a characterization akin to that of von Renesse and Sturm, demonstrating our lower bounds on Ricci curvature as the Ricci curvature of the associated path-metric space using the Wasserstein-2 distance. A key outcome of this approach is proving a discrete version of the Bakry-Emry formula.

Recently, Natural Language Processing (NLP) has seen significant advancements, with word embeddings emerging as a crucial factor in this evolution. While coding-mixing (mixing different languages within a sentence or text) is a common occurrence in the Indian subcontinent, existing NLTools, including word-embedding models, have focused primarily on single-language datasets. Consequently, there is currently no resource available for creating word embeddings specifically from code-mixed content. This limitation hinders the development of effective NLP tools and resources for the Indian region. Our study addresses this gap by proposing a methodology to generate word-embedding models using only text that contains multiple linguistic codes. We evaluate the performance of our model against single-language benchmarks using standard evaluation metrics and identify limitations in our approach. Through this work, we have made the dataset and the resulting model publicly available to support future research.

Using a pressure of 160 GPa, we utilized the quasi-harmonic approximation to model atomic positions, resulting in an optimized $T_{c}$ of 202 K. This value aligns closely with experimental measurements and earlier theoretical studies. We introduce a method designed to differentiate between correlated and causally linked findings in genome-wide association studies (GWA). While current techniques like Genomic Control provide a global correction for population structure, they fail to address confounding variables on a global scale; our approach targets specific causal inference. The foundation of this work lies in modeling the joint distribution of genotypes and associated statistics using Hidden Markov Models, followed by identifying locally consistent phenotypic patterns that validate causal relationships. The entire inference framework is implemented in a user-friendly R package available at https://github.com/andrewzack/LocalCT.

This paper introduces a new approach to designing quasi-static walking mechanisms for space-constrained bipedal robots. These systems utilize thrusters to apply impulsive vertical forces to the environment, facilitating a robot capable of moving through restricted areas where traditional swing-based walking is infeasible. Impulse-based control theory is employed to compute the state transitions resulting from these force impulses. The work also presents a systematic method for optimizing walking parameters to achieve maximum elevation. Additionally, we outline an algorithm for autonomously planning walking routes that incorporates these optimized parameters. Simulations validating this bipedal system's effectiveness in both impulsive traversal and route planning will be provided.

We introduce SuRe, an open-source framework designed to estimate poses and enable visual relocalization using dense 3D surface units (surfels). The surfel map is constructed by fusing depth and normal data from multiple dense 3D scans. To facilitate efficient tracking, the 3D surfels are projected onto a rigid body that moves with the camera, forming a co-moving coordinate system. Within this setup, both the camera and surfels are represented as spheres; self-calculations between them allow for the derivation of a cost function that enforces geometric consistency. A non-linear optimization process minimizes this cost to enable real-time pose estimation with high accuracy. SuRe is particularly well-suited for semi-automated tasks such as robot assembly, where its pre-existing 3D model knowledge is leveraged to enhance pose detection. A web portal allows users to upload their own 3D models and interact with the system.

Federated learning enables collaborative model training across a distributed set of devices, each holding its own local dataset. A significant challenge arises when clients possess only partial labels for their data, necessitating methods to integrate this incomplete information without violating privacy constraints. This paper introduces a novel framework that treats unlabeled data points as observations from the same probabilistic distribution as the labeled points within each client. By employing an Expectation-Maximization algorithm, the study derives closed-form solutions for this estimation process. A key advantage of this approach lies in its minimal additional computational overhead compared to scenarios with full labeling. Furthermore, the paper examines the impact of probability parameter estimation on each client and presents validation results on real-world datasets that demonstrate the superiority of this method over current state-of-the-art approaches.

The dynamical accretion disk generated in the late phase of a black hole-neutron star merger is a key determinant of the resulting jet properties and the associated electromagnetic counterparts. This disk arises from the combined effects of tidal disruption and the direct accretion of unbound material. This study examines the mass evolution of this disk through numerical-relativity-based simulations, comparing them against analytical models that incorporate both tidal disruption and direct accretion. We find a strong agreement between simulation data and predictions, with a model parameter $f_{\rm td}$ of approximately 0.025 accurately describing the disk mass for non-spinning black holes ($a=0$) with masses between 5 and $30 M_\odot$, and for black holes of $5 M_\odot$ with spins up to $a=0.9$. Furthermore, we propose a simple formula to estimate the minimum black hole mass capable of completely accreting a neutron star's tidal debris without forming a disk; this formula applies to dimensionless spin values exceeding 0.25.

The primary goal of this note is to exhibit a specific invariant measure for the meta-process, from which a non-trivial invariant measure for the in-progress process can be derived; this intermediate measure allows the construction of a QSD. While QDs are typically associated with absorption events, our approach establishes one without referencing absorption. The theoretical proof relies on two key properties: the ability to reset and the system's good mixing behavior. Both properties are satisfied by the stochastic Ginzburg-Landau (SGL) process. We verify these properties using explicit computations of stochastic resets and matrix exponentials, which supports the construction of a QSD. The resulting measure is shown to be invariant, confirming that a QSD exists.

This research investigates the optical binding within a dimer of dielectric particles positioned proximate to a graphene sheet. Employing the multipole expansion approach for field expansion and the T-matrix method for scattering analysis, we demonstrate that surface plasmon excitations on graphene substantially alter the spacing between bound particles. Our computational results indicate that adjusting the chemical potential of graphene enables the optical binding distances to be actively controlled. Furthermore, we anticipate that this mechanism will facilitate the optical assembly of dielectric structures using plasmon-active two-dimensional materials beyond graphene, including other plasmon-supporting sheets.

This study investigates whether extending the duration that abdominal pain patients remain in the Emergency Department (ED) can effectively lower admission rates. The paper posits that for certain individuals experiencing abdominal pain, a more comprehensive diagnostic evaluation necessitates a longer stay than the standard protocol allows. To explore this, the authors developed a flow-cytometry-inspired model representing the temporal distribution of patient movements between the ED and inpatient care. The model's parameters were estimated using data from 1,000 patients with abdominal pain who visited the University of Michigan's Freestanding Emergency Services between 2014 and 2015. The findings indicate that the proposed framework provides an excellent fit for the observed discharge and admission time distributions. The study's main conclusion is that increasing the maximum time patients can stay in the department is likely to decrease the number of admissions. The authors suggest that implementing this strategy could assist emergency departments in managing bed inventories more effectively.

We introduce a novel mathematical framework for formalizing task execution within environmental contexts involving multiple agents. This model represents an interaction between the two as coupled ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and redefines a utility function that unifies the perspectives of all agents into a single social welfare view. Under specific technical conditions, we prove the existence of at least one Nash equilibrium, demonstrating that the resulting dynamics can be decomposed as coupled gradient ODEs with respect to individual agents' unique metrics. Subsequently, we extend this advanced modeling approach from constant vector fields to scenarios involving time-varying tasks.

Charge-dependent azimuthal momentum correlations, arising from phenomena such as the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME) and the Chiral Magnetic Wave (CMW), serve as key experimental signatures in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. This study presents new calculations of these CME/CMW charge-dependent correlations, specifically the triangle ($\gamma$) and four-particle ($\gamma_{ST}$) streams, across a range of LHC energy settings. By expressing these observables as functions of transverse momentum ($k_T$) and system size, and incorporating finite quark masses and realistic hadron spectrum densities, we estimate the magnitude of these signals for various centralities at the LHC. Furthermore, we analyze the distinct contributions from different particle species to these correlations and draw implications for the Chiral Magnetic Wave based on these LHC predictions.

The rise of crowdfunding has transformed into a highly competitive landscape where securing funding is essential for launching new ventures. Although existing literature examines various strategies to improve campaign outcomes, there remains a significant scarcity of research specifically addressing the role of investor behavior in shaping these results. This study utilizes a large-scale dataset comprising nearly 150,000 crowdfunding projects to analyze follower dynamics and their impact on success. By employing advanced data mining and statistical techniques, we identify specific behavioral signals of followers and assess their distinct contributions to funding achievement. Our findings reveal that the mere act of funding a project does not guarantee success; rather, prospective funders exhibit specific behaviors prior to investment that serve as meaningful indicators of favorable outcomes. These insights carry significant implications for entrepreneurs, project leaders, and platforms seeking to enhance funding acquisition rates.

While machine learning offers promising solutions for detecting network attacks, the necessity of integrating data from diverse sources to identify sophisticated attacks introduces significant challenges, specifically the heterogeneous nature of these data streams and the extensive volumes involved. This study addresses these issues by employing discrete multi-valued logic (DMVL) as a method to aggregate various data sources, effectively mitigating both problems. We propose a novel DMVL-driven ensemble framework designed for speed and simplicity, utilizing logical operations to evaluate evidence across multiple data sources and determine the most probable attack type. Unlike traditional ensemble techniques that depend on a standard classification step, our approach uses multi-valued logic directly for inference. Furthermore, the framework accelerates processing by offloading work to parallel systems through DMVL's intrinsic capabilities. We implemented and tested this framework using DMVL's C++ semantic definition alongside binary vector representations for attack and connection data on a cluster of work nodes. This representation streamlined both the data representation scheme and the DMVL computational processes. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed solution outperforms two established classification methods in terms of accuracy, as well as scalability and performance when operated via DMVL's C++ interpreter in parallel environments.

Optimating a sequence of tasks, where each task may involve multiple constraints, allows a robot to perform operations ranging from collision-free planning to the integration of numerous sensor data within a unified framework. This paper specifically addresses the offline optimization of these tasks for a serial manipulator in real-time, or sequentially. To achieve this, we formulates a mathematical problem to determine the most suitable task priorities, which is then resolved using the Out-of-the-box Out-of-sample optimization (O2O2) algorithm. The approach is validated on two distinct scenarios: the first involves a planar three-link arm navigating an environment with multiple obstacles, and the second simulates a surgical procedure featuring a non-planar, haptically constrained movement around a hidden cavity.

The interface between semiconductors and their barrier layers plays a critical role in defining the performance of electrostatic gates within electrostatic environment for quantum bits. To address this, the study employs ab initio density functional theory to analyze the interface between the topological insulator Bi$_2$Se$_3$ and graphene, a material often used to truncate topological insulators. The researchers identify specific graphene orientations that maximize electron mobility at this interface, finding parallel values of approximately 10,000 cm$^2$/Vs—comparable to the highest reported mobilities for topological insulator-semiconductor junctions. The study further investigates the underlying scattering mechanisms, identifying phonon interactions as the primary constraint on achieving this high mobility. These findings suggest that moving forward, the field should prioritize reducing defect densities and phonon populations to push interface mobilities beyond 10,000 cm$^2$/Vs, thereby creating superior platforms for qubit use.

Group synchronization refers to the coexistence of multiple distinct temporal evolutions within a network of coupled oscillators, where each cluster of synchrony shares the same local dynamics. While extensive progress has been made in fully symmetric systems regarding the stability of these clusters, systems with complex, heterogeneous symmetries remain largely unexplored. This paper addresses that gap by analyzing the stability of group synchronization manifolds specifically within odd-cyclic asymmetrical ring networks. Our findings extend previous research limited to two-cyclic symmetries. Specifically, we derive sufficient conditions ensuring the asymptotic stability of all possible group synchronization patterns in these odd-cyclic structures. To validate our theoretical framework, we present the results of a numerical simulation.

This paper investigates how Western natural language search engines process video queries and retrieve relevant content. Researchers conducted experiments in English and Spanish to evaluate (i) result diversity, (ii) semantic relatedness among results, and (iii) visual and textual relevance. The study's primary conclusion is that, for Spanish speakers, the linguistic characteristics of queries significantly influence the personalization of search results, causing Spanish queries to exhibit stronger semantic clustering and lower diversity compared to English. Furthermore, there is a notable disconnect between textual and visual relevance, particularly with Spanish content, indicating that search engines often prioritize popular or branded channels over the user's intent.

To investigate supersymmetric monodromy defects within the critical Wess-Zumino model in four dimensions, we employ analytical bootstrap methodologies. Our methodology begins by generalizing the analytic bootstrap to include the presence of a defect, resulting in a set of key constraints on the function $\mathcal{F}_{\Delta,\bar{\Delta}}(u)$, which characterizes four-point correlation functions. Specifically, we demonstrate that the expansion of this amplitude around the infinite separation limit rigorously enforces the spin-structure of the operator spectrum. Building on this, we extend the computation of $\mathcal{F}_{\Delta,\bar{\Delta}}(u)$ to the intermediate regime and derive additional constraints. Finally, leveraging these findings, we initiate an inaugural analytical bootstrap procedure for a correlation-driven defect conformal field theory.

This study investigates the impact of interference correlation on local delay within correlated ALOHA systems. We begin by establishing a unified framework that encapsulates both independent ALOHA and correlated ALOHA protocols. Building upon this model, we analytically derive the mean delay and the mean squared delay for these networks. To solve the coupled non-linear equations inherent in the delay characterization, we employ an Newton-based numerical method. Additionally, we introduce a closed-form linear approximation for delay that simplifies analysis. The article further examines key characteristics of delay under correlated ALOHA and, through comparative analysis with independent ALOHA, highlights performance distinctions. Finally, the proposed linear approximation and the numerical solution method are validated against simulation data.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are highly effective for node classification tasks, yet they often falter when confronted with extremely limited training data per class. Although various techniques have been developed to enhance graph label propagation, they typically demand multiple label-remodeling iterations to achieve satisfactory performance. To address this challenge, this paper introduces InpoGraph, a framework designed to assign pseudo-labels with "high utility" during the early stages of supervision to aid parameter refinement and prevent the model from propagating erroneous information. Specifically, the authors define the difficult concept of neighbor nodes that emit negative signals as node poisoners and propose a poisoners-suppression mechanism to neutralize their impact. Furthermore, the framework integrates a custom loss function that incorporates a penalty term, ensuring the model prioritizes positive predictions. Empirical evaluations on six real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach substantially outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in scenarios involving sparse labels, all while requiring only a single pass.

Accurately capturing local details is fundamental to understanding videos, a principle underlying many biological visual recognition systems. Aligning with this, we introduce Patchwise Fractal ResNet (PFRNet), a video recognition architecture that learns features from patches rather than individual pixels. PFRNet achieves this by integrating fractal structures with the ResNet model, creating multiple self-similar zooming tiers that progressively refine from local areas to global context. Experiments on the UCF101 and UCF-NED24-11 datasets reveal significant improvements with PFRNet, which outperforms current methods and is particularly effective at lower resolutions. Additionally, our model demonstrates strong generalization capabilities when applied to unseen low-resolution variants of videos.

This research investigates the non-equilibrium time-dependent dynamics of a one-dimensional gas consisting of $N$ particles interacting through two-body repulsive interactions under external confining potentials. Focusing on the large-scale limit, the study applies a macroscopic limit procedure to derive a closed-form differential equation governing the time evolution of the one-particle marginal density. By leveraging this theory, the paper presents methods for the numerical simulation of one- and two-dimensional cases, demonstrating that the predicted results align well with Monte Carlo simulations and theoretical expectations.

This study investigates Green Communication in mobile data networks by integrating simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT) with precancellation techniques on the receiver end. Focused on a point-to-point frequency-selective channel utilizing an OFDM framework, the research examines a scenario where an information receiver (IR) and a power receiver (PR) are present. Both the IR and the PR utilize time-switching (TS) based reception. At the PR, received signals are processed to remove the component intended for the IR before the signal is routed to the power harvesting circuit. Similarly, the IR applies the received wave to eliminate the portion directed at the PR prior to extracting the desired information. By employing receiver precancellation, the transmitter is relieved of the burden of knowing the PR's channel state information (CSI). Consequently, channel power allocation is managed solely by the transmitter to maximize the PR's harvest while meeting the IR's signal quality requirements via receiver cabling. If the TS fraction for the PR is too limited, the power injected into the PR becomes unnecessary excess. Therefore, the optimization targets the TS fraction and channel power allocation to maximize green efficiency while ensuring the IR's rate constraints are satisfied. The problem is formulated as a non-convex optimization task that is ultimately resolved using an efficient iterative algorithm.

This work reports on a spin-imbalanced Fermi gas characterized by a contact interaction, situated in the regime of both weak and strong interactions. The spin-population ratio $P_{F}$ is a key variable, and we observe a first-order phase transition occurring at a critical point $P_{F}^{C}$. As the system moves from the weak to the strong interaction limit, this critical point shifts to lower values of $P_{F}$. Furthermore, we have established a novel ferromagnetic state where the system exhibits absolute spin polarization ($P_{F}=0$) under strong interactions. The findings are analyzed using the weak-interaction Chiral Gross-Pitavskii equation, and we offer a theoretical explanation for the spin polarization driven by the Pauli exclusion principle. These properties are also contrasted with the predictions of the strong-interaction Ferromagnetic state proposed by Coddington and Thomas.

This study introduces a novel configuration in microwave optomechanics where a parallel RLC circuit serves as the mechanical oscillator. The oscillator's mass analog is the energy stored in capacitance, which modifies at a classical level through interaction with inductance and capacitance components while experiencing quantal fluctuations at the quantum scale. We also propose a planar architecture to realize this system. By applying an external microwave tone field, we achieve sideband absorption and emission, enabling quantal cooling of the magnetotic mass-motion of the fluctuating circuit elements.

This work investigates sem-classical orthogonal polynomials derived from a generalised Airy weight, $w(x)=\exp(-\frac{x^{3}}{3}+ax+b)x^{-\frac{2}{3}\gamma}$, defined for $x\in[0,\infty)$, where $\gamma>\!-\frac{2}{3}\gamma$ is a real parameter. The study determines biorthogonal polynomials and their corresponding polynomials of the first kind, demonstrating that both families satisfy the same second-order differential equation. Furthermore, several properties regarding these polynomial systems are examined.

This work demonstrates that simple rule-based autonomous mobile robots can spontaneously produce complex behaviors, including veering away from walls and forming stable traveling waves within narrow corridors. We implement this investigation using the `fugue` platform, a system designed to analyze biological pattern formation. The observed phenomena emerge from a dynamic tension between two forces: short-range repulsion triggered by wall detection and a long-range alignment mechanism linking individual orientations. This configuration creates conditions analogous to the hydrodynamics of sheep-alfalfa systems described by Tomohiro Nishiwaki and colleagues in *Physical Review E*, specifically the motion of animal-orientation waves. Our results indicate that the `fugue` simulation successfully generates traveling waves with velocities and wavelengths closely matching those reported in the animal study, while also enabling robust exploration of the parameter space governing collective behavior.

This paper introduces various chiral observables for two-dimensional conformal field theories defined on globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifolds. The study focuses particularly on the optical disc within the 2-dimensional de Sitter context and provides both theories and examples for these non-local, specifically chiral, measurements.

Laparoscopic surgery presents a significant challenge due to the three-dimensional nature of the visual input provided by their cameras. *In* this paper, *we* introduce novel techniques designed for the removal of smoke during laparoscopy, which includes a method based on characterizing smoke using RGB information and another utilizing depth maps. *We* also present the *only publicly available*, smoke-annotated dataset for laparoscopy, which has been created through the meticulous manual labeling of烟 points in 1,000 smoke-affected frames sourced from the LS3 dataset. *We* have made this dataset accessible for research purposes. *We* have evaluated the proposed methods using quantitative and qualitative metrics, which have been used to determine the most effective smoke removal solution. *We* have also conducted an extensive user study involving the assessment of video restoration quality post-smoke removal by a group of 17 surgeons.

This study evaluates the viability of achieving frequency robustness in multi-qubit trapped-ion quantum circuits by utilizing long-axis vibrational modes for multi-frequency microwave-driven quantum operations. Our analysis focuses on Rabi oscillations and two-qubit gates involving pairs of ions driven by microwaves parallel to the trap long axis. We assess system resilience across various coupling regimes—weak, intermediate, and strong—demonstrating that effective quantum gates are achievable in all instances. Specifically, within the intermediate coupling regime, the required detuning for full Raman-like resonance increases significantly due to mode coupling structures, yet complete resonance can still be achieved through compensation provided by proper long-range ion confinement. Our simulations indicate that high-fidelity quantum gates are realizable assuming current levels of technical performance in state preparation, control pulses, and readout.

We introduce an efficient and accurate method for modeling the structural phase transition in barium titanate (BaTiO$_3$) using ab initio lattice dynamics (LDM). This framework decouples the complex, high-dimensional phase space transition into manageable subspaces defined by a few key order parameters, yielding the structural prototypes: cubic (Pm$\overline{3}$m), tetragonal (P4mm), and rhombohedral ($R\overline{3}m$). The proposed LDM scheme effectively captures anharmonic effects across all three phases, enabling the calculation of soft-mode frequencies along the transition path and the identification of the dominant tilting modes that drive phase changes in BaTiO$_3$. Furthermore, solving the partition function over this decoupled lattice dynamics configuration space offers a systematic and accessible route to computing free energy surfaces relative to the relevant order parameters. When tested on the well-studied $\text{BaTiO}_3$ system, our results align closely with previous ${{\text{G}}\omega}$ calculations and experimental data. Finally, the universal nature of this method in capturing structural physics makes it highly applicable to other complex phase transitions in perovskite materials.

Multivariate functional or spatial data are frequently encountered in the natural sciences. This article introduces new Gaussian graphical models tailored for such data and outlines methods to determine their parameters. The validity of these approaches rests on the assumption that the processes are stationary and can be represented using Fourier series. Under this framework, and with only a minimal set of parameters defining the graph structure, we employ an information-criterion framework to identify conditional independence relations between realizations. The methodology is demonstrated within the context of analyzing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data related to motor tasks.

Current quantum processors suffer from constraints including restricted qubit counts, connectivity limits, and coherence times, which necessitates that computations be confined to a small number of gates. Preserving quantum advantage requires cleverly leveraging quantum properties throughout lengthy algorithms to optimize resource usage. This paper proposes using dynamic programming (DP) to optimize quantum advantage by (i) decomposing an algorithm into distinct functional sections and (ii) applying DP techniques to each segment for such improvements as qubit reduction, automatic section balancing for even load distribution across error-corrected segments, and more uniform noise exposure. The methodology is demonstrated using two quantum simulations—reflected amplitude encoding (RAE) for Hermitian eigenvalue estimation and the HHL algorithm—as well as via the SWAP test for state overlap estimation to illustrate how DP effectively (i) enhances qubit efficiency through quicker, more accurate simulations and (ii) increases the total gate count while actually lowering the total resources needed.

This study examines how to minimize quadratic functions on random, symmetric matrices, specifically looking at scenarios where the eigenvalues of the Hessian matrix cluster near the boundaries of the spectral distribution. This spectral behavior is observed in significant classes of combinatorial optimization problems, such as those involving the boundary of the polynomial threshold set, particularly when the Hessian is doubly stochastic. While standard eigenvalues are well-documented, our observations focus heavily on the structure of these edge-concentrated components. For matrices following a sparse, symmetric model, we demonstrate that the count of distinct eigenvalues is $O(\log(1/\epsilon))$, provided the off-diagonal entries are $O(1/n)$. Additionally, we identify that the eigenvalues within such clusters are uniformly distributed, and the associated eigenspaces possess high dimensionality. These findings suggest that the Riemannian manifold optimization method, which operates on the Hessian's principal components, is highly effective. Specifically, we establish that the sparsity level of the matrix can be approximated using just $O(\log(1/\epsilon))$ principal components.

Using many-body perturbation theory combined with the random phase approximation, we have calculated the binding energies of inter- and intralayer excitonic biexcitons in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides. We find that biexciton formation is significantly favored by large layer polarizations and small layers thicknesses. Specifically, our calculations show binding energies of approximately 0.3 eV for intralayer biexcitons and 0.2 eV for interlayer biexcitons. These strong binding interactions persist at room temperature, indicating potential applications for excitonic devices. We also identified characteristic moiré patterns in the binding energies of interlayer excitonic biexcitons as functions of separation distance and floating charge neutrality point.

This paper introduces a high-precision indoor positioning algorithm based on received signal strength (RSS), specifically designed to multipath effects. The core innovation lies in leveraging the information contained within multipath components (MPCs) to bootstrap the initialization of a particle filter (PF). By integrating a radiating source image with a direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimator, the proposed method identifies the angles of the strongest peaks to isolate multipath signals. The DOA data is subsequently converted into a set of probable tag positions, which serve as PF initial states by restricting the starting probability distribution. This approach significantly reduces search complexity and mitigates the risk of prolonged position drift. Experimental validation indicates that the method achieves an average positioning accuracy of 15.9 cm, representing approximately a 60% reduction in error compared to traditional PF, while also decreasing the computational cost associated with processing the arrival time.

The study reports a paired, simultaneous production of two longitudinally polarized vector bosons in the $vB\to WZ$ process, utilizing proton-proton collision data from the LHC at 13 TeV collected by the ATLAS detector. The analysis utilizes a total dataset corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 36.1 fb$^{-−1}$ across the di-photon plus $WW$ final state channel. The resulting data exhibits agreement with Standard Model predictions regarding the polarization characteristics of the $W$ bosons. Measurements are reported for the normalized cross-sections as functions of the boson transverse momenta, comparing the data with next-to-leading-order QCD predictions. The measurement's statistical significance for the observed di-photon plus $WW$ production reaches 5.2 standard deviations.

The analysis demonstrates that the Cotton tensor can characterize gravitational phenomena more effectively than the full Einstein tensor within the framework of general relativity. By examining a specific instance involving a spin-0 field coupled to gravity, the Cotton tensor captures the interaction between the spin-0 field and gravity with greater clarity. Consequently, this field of coupling appears distinct from the self-interaction of the spin-0 field. The finding suggests that including the Cotton tensor in the gravity action at the quantum level could yield novel insights into cosmological problems.

This text outlines an ordered class of spectral spaces termed orthomodular spaces, defined through continuous, discrete, and clopen (complemented and open) functions. The author demonstrates that the structures of these spaces are equally captured by orthomodular frames—frames that are both completely distributive and equipped with an orthogonality relation—which also allows for the formulation of key frame theoretic results specific to this context.

This paper presents a visual proof explorer for formal proofs developed within the Coq proof assistant. By generating flowchart-style diagrams that map proof strategies, this tool supports proof analysis and verification. We have integrated this visualization capability directly into the Lean Coq extension to enable features such as interactive proof stepping, the export of PDF diagrams, and in-compiler type signature display. Empirical testing indicates significant utility for proof inspection, particularly when used as an instructional aid.

Our approach employs subconvexity estimates derived from recent progress on 20th and fourth-degree GL(2) automorphic instances of the Rankin-Selbeck method, as developed by S. Kim and J. Shin. Our estimated bound for the 4th moment aligns with existing subconvexity bounds for 20th degree GL(2) problems. Our strategy can be generalized to compute moments of arbitrary length for automorphic forms of all levels and weights, provided the associated L-functions satisfy the RH hypothesis.

In this paper, novel adaptive intelligent L\'{u}cvik-like (LLL) methods are proposed to pre-condition intricate symmetric positive definite equations derived from the Finite Difference Method applied to Laplace's equation. Subsequently, the output of these adaptive LLL pre-conditioners is utilized as an initial estimate to significantly decrease the number of iterations required by an ILS solver. Numerical experiments confirm that this hybrid algorithm exhibits superior performance compared to standard approaches. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's stability, accuracy, and computational efficiency was conducted, supported by comparative studies against other existing methods.

The Incident Reporting System (IRS) is a web-based platform designed to gather accounts from individuals who have witnessed incidents involving intelligent systems. Such reports, which may involve autonomous vehicles or robotic assistance, serve as valuable data for training intelligence systems to identify and avoid similar future incidents. Each incident account includes metadata like the reporter's location and the date the event occurred.

The gradient flow exhibits a striking parallel to the coarse-graining principle inherent to the Renormalization Group (RG). Within the framework of the Wilson action under covariant exact RG, scalar field theories are linked with the gradient flow of simple field theories. A key insight arises from solving the coarse-graining flow equations for the Wilson action: these solutions can be expressed as the fine-graining reversal applied to the gradient flow solution of a "simple" action modified by specific flow-dependent couplings, such as a dimensionless mass. Leveraging this structure provides novel perspectives on the connection between the gradient flow and the beta function, particularly regarding its dimensionless mass parameter. Furthermore, this approach allows the determination of non-perturbative solutions for the Wilson action's evolution with respect to the gradient flow scale, with significant applications in the analysis of the theory's dimensionless mass behavior at short distances.

Although the American Heart Association's 2011 guidelines recommend statin therapy for primary prevention in middle-aged adults with diabetes, individual patient factors often complicate its application. To better understand real-world adherence, researchers analyzed clinical notes from 1,000 adult primary care visits at a Boston clinic between 2009 and 2010. The study utilized Natural Language Processing (NLP) to identify mentions of statins and structured data to extract patient risk metrics. Findings revealed statins were mentioned in about 25% of visits. The text mentions frequently addressed patient barriers such as fear of cancer or organ failure, the high cost of medication, and lack of insurance coverage. Conversely, visits often omitted risk assessments for cholesterol or statin benefits. These results indicate that clinical notes effectively capture both the prevalence of statin discussions and the specific considerations doctors make during patient consultations.

This study introduces a matrix-based approach to examine a non-universal two-dimensional percolation model featuring a square lattice and a coordination number of z=4. In this framework, a site remains occupied with a site-dependent probability $p_i$ if the corresponding site matrix $M_i$ is non-zero. We demonstrate that the model's average site-occupation probability, $\langle p \rangle$, is strictly governed by the matrices' average $ \langle M \rangle $ and their second moment $\langle M^2 \rangle$. Given that the model exhibits both ordinary and extreme eigenvalues, we investigate how these values influence percolation behavior. Our findings confirm that the system follows standard scaling laws characterized by the ordinary critical exponent $\beta = 1/2$. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of eigenvalue extremes on the system's upper and lower critical exponents.

We introduce a theory of atom-cavity mediated entanglement-induced interaction, applicable to both one- and two-atom systems. This interaction arises from the exchange of virtual photons and exhibits exponential growth, analogous to the exchange mediated by virtual phonons. The proposed model effectively reinterprets the atom-cavity coupling regime under the framework of exchange-induced interactions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the entanglement-induced interaction between atoms can be tuned to achieve the universal quantum control of atoms, including simulation of the Ising model via a von Neumann measurement protocol.

De novo genome assembly involves reconstructing a complete genome from a collection of short DNA fragments, a process fundamental to modern biology for generating genomic data. While existing methods often struggle with genomes containing repetitive elements—where they incorrectly model overlaps as single occurrences—we introduce a new model that accurately represents these cases. By leveraging the powerful SASPY framework, this approach is solved using semi-analytic techniques and the minimum tiling path algorithm on a genome graph, which is proven to be isomorphic to the original genome when repetition length is accounted for. The SASPIPI model effectively captures standard biological data characteristics and can be seamlessly extended to include multiple samples, thereby validating its robustness for real-world genomic analysis.

The delayed logistic equation serves as a foundational model for analyzing oscillatory behavior in ecological systems. While previous research has primarily utilized linearization techniques to demonstrate the emergence of a stable limit cycle as equation parameters vary, this study offers a distinct perspective. We adopt a conceptual framework grounded in a time-lag representing the period between resource depletion and the subsequent regulatory response. Leveraging the classical theory of analytic functions to model this lag, which can be approximated by a finite series of exponential terms, we examine system behavior. This theoretical approach yields an understanding of how the system oscillates and the conditions under which these oscillations stabilize.

We introduce an innovative statistical approach for modeling temporal point processes. By leveraging Comberi's $l_1$-median depth to measure outlier magnitude, our method constructs models that effectively capture the typical patterns of the data. Consequently, this framework allows researchers to understand the standard behavior of time-stamped events. In addition to model formulation, we describe parameter estimation techniques based on maximum likelihood principles. Our contributions are validated through extensive experiments using both simulated datasets and real-world applications, demonstrating the model's efficacy and robustness.

Quantum systems have emerged as highly effective platforms for thermal machines, with their unique properties enabling performance that classical devices cannot match. Within the field of quantum thermodynamics, understanding these systems through geometric perspectives offers a powerful analytical tool. This approach facilitates the formulation of general thermodynamic laws and enables the design of specific machines. Previous geometric studies have largely centered on isolated (unitary) processes, whereas understanding the role of non-unitary dynamics is crucial for practical thermal devices. In response, this paper introduces a general relationship linking the rate of available work production in machine cycles to Kähler currents, providing the foundation for geometric thermodynamics of open quantum systems. The model is validated through detailed analysis of a two-level system operating as a quantum heat engine, with specific attention given to the quantum four-stroke Otto cycle.

The lifetime measurements for the $2^+$ $\rightarrow$ $0^+$ gamma transitions in $^{69}$Ge and $^{71}$Ge were conducted using the laser-ion trap method. By employing a relative recoil method, the collective characteristics of ground states in these isotopes were derived, yielding magnetic moments ($\mu_\mathrm{g}$) of $+0.699(10)\,\mu_\mathrm{N}$/$-0.703(10)\,\mu_\mathrm{N}$ and quadrupole moments ($Q_\mathrm{g}$) of $+190(14)\ \mathrm{b}$/$-200(14)\ \mathrm{b}$ for $^{69}$Ge/$^{71}$Ge respectively. A comparative analysis with magnetic quadrupole moments from $^{70}$Ge ($\mu=+0.769(12)\,\mu_\mathrm{N}$/$Q=+190(14)\ \mathrm{b}$) reveals a systematic progression, suggesting a consistent geometric deformation across the $A\approx70$ region of the nuclear chart.

This work presents results from the CRYSTAL project, which marks the inaugural application of ion trap-based isochronous secular cooling for measuring the masses of short-lived exotic nuclei with high precision. Nuclei produced via the ISOLDE facility at CERN were transported through the ISOLTRAP facility, where the novel secular cooling strategy was employed to achieve exact mass determinments for transient isotopes. Using this approach, the first measurements of ion cyclotron resonance frequencies and relative masses were completed for $^{39}$Ar, $^{40}$Ar, $^{41}$Ar, $^{42}$Ar, $^{43}$Ar, $^{45}$Ca, $^{47}$Ca, $^{48}$Ca, $^{49}$Ca, $^{51}$Cr, $^{54}$Cr, $^{55}$Mn, $^{57}$Fe, $^{58}$Fe, $^{60}$Ni, $^{62}$Ni, $^{64}$Ni, $^{65}$Cu, $^{67}$Zn, $^{68}$Zn, $^{70}$Zn, $^{72}$Ge, $^{74}$Ge, $^{76}$Ge, $^{82}$Sr, $^{87}$Sr, $^{88}$Sr, $^{90}$Z

We present a method for extracting Boltzmann distributions from lattice field theories that do not depend on ensembles. This approach applies the "fixed point" algorithm to a Monte Carlo dynamics flow, employing the same-configuration acceptance-criterion. In this context, the flow algorithm acts as an operator, and a configuration is considered fixed when applying the operator yields no changes. Since the distribution of such invariant configurations aligns with the desired Boltzmann distribution, this distribution is used to compute ensemble-averages. This strategy obviates the necessity of generating representative configurations from a specific prior distribution that already embodies the flow's properties. We demonstrate the method with $SU(2)$ and fundamental $SU(3)$ lattice gauge theories and provide evidence that the resulting distributions closely approximate those of the standard heat-bath algorithm.

Regular expressions, or regexes, offer a potent mechanism for defining patterns in structured or formatted text. Frequently employed in natural language processing and full-stack development, they are utilized to parse forms, organize unstructured content, detect spam, and perform search and replace operations. Although manual creation remains the standard, this process demands both specialized knowledge and considerable effort. We introduce an innovative approach that streamlines pattern recognition through the use of images to train "image-to-regex" models. By converting the task of crafting regular expressions into a classification problem, this method taps into significant advancements in deep learning for image recognition. The model learns to map specific visual patterns directly to their corresponding regex equivalents. The system involves two phases: first, training a deep neural network to classify text patterns within images, and second, converting the resulting class probabilities into optimized regex syntax. The output is a set of "image-based" expressions capable of performing text matching equivalent to hand-written counterparts, as verified by experiments showing these generated regexes achieve high accuracy.

A search for the two-body decay of dark matter particles via the $Z$ boson was conducted using a dataset of 139$\text{ fb}^{-1}$ collected by the CMS detector at the LHC. The analysis examined proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV recorded during the 2016, 2017, and 2018 runs. A single-lepton and missing transverse momentum signature was examined, with a focus on events containing one electron or one muon. The event selection targets a specific topology characterized by high values of missing transverse momentum, the transverse momentum of the isolated lepton, and the recoil against it. The analysis did not detect any statistically significant excess above background expectations. These observations are consistent with standard model predictions, allowing for exclusion limits on the proposed decay mechanism. Specifically, at a 95\% confidence level, this process is excluded for a dark matter mass ranging from 2 to 45 GeV. Furthermore, assuming the two-body hypothesis holds and using the framework of effective field theory, constraints were derived for several operators governing interactions between the $Z$ boson and dark matter.

This study introduces an architecture for text-to-SQL semantic parsing designed to mitigate over-smoothing effects inherent in attention-based encoders while leveraging pre-trained language models. Recognizing that attention mechanisms can cause distinct SQL representations to converge into nearly identical outputs, thereby hindering fine-grained control, we incorporate a pre-trained language model to robustly encode contextual information. Additionally, we address limitations in existing decoders regarding the handling of fine-grained semantics within database schema terms, such as column names, which often lack discriminative power. To resolve this, we implement a two-stage SQL generator: first extracting and ordering relevant schema columns, then constructing the final SQL query. This proposed two-part approach, implemented within Cross-BERT and TwoPartSQL, was validated against two prominent benchmarks, Spider and SQLEVAL, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance.

The LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey (LoTSS) offers a comprehensive radio mapping of the northern hemisphere, serving as an essential survey for studying cosmological structure and the evolution of galaxies. The first installment, LoTSS Dr1, encompasses the region north of $\delta = 0^{\circ}$; however, this coverage is fragmented by gaps resulting from the scheduling constraints of the observatory. To optimize data utility, we present an improved segmentation of Dr1 that aligns with quality standards and minimizes segment dimensions. By refining the original segments to create smaller tiles, we enhance survey exploitation through a novel approach tested with mock catalogs. Using the Dragonfly16 catalog, which features realistic source distributions, we evaluated our methodology. The results demonstrate that this technique increases the recovered completeness by an average of 10\% and the position accuracy by an additional 2\%. These findings are expected to translate to similar gains when applied to the forthcoming full LoTSS release.

The high-dimensional rank lasso (HDR LASSO) model was developed to handle high-dimensional data analysis tasks, specifically addressing multivariate regression and enhanced rank correlation. We demonstrate that hierarchical clustering based on the squared d² Hilbert-Schmidt distance between row-wise Gram matrices of the HDR LASSO estimator effectively identifies the true labels in a multivariate setting. Our analysis establishes strong theoretical backing for this approach, proving it possesses strong consistency almost sure convergence characteristics. Empirical results indicate that this method outperforms both established and contemporary algorithms.

We examine open systems operating within nonequilibrium settings and generate entropy. Using methods from $\Gamma$-calculus, we show that the entropy production functional is convex, which identifies all globally optimal control protocols for its maximization. This result also establishes a useful variational formula for the rate of entropy change. Applying these findings, we first derive a criterion to verify if a specific protocol achieves global optimality. Second, we utilize the formula developed in the first part of this work, along with an additional assumption, to construct optimal protocols for specific cases, such as maximizing the efficiency of heat engines and the power output during the charging of electrical capacitors.
