Deforming the integration contours offers a method to alleviate the sign problem encountered by Monte Carlo simulations. This study applies such a deformation to the Fermi-Hubbard model filling the range from nearly full to nearly empty states. Surprisingly, the intensity of the sign problem proves symmetrical with respect to filling number ($\delta$), contradicting earlier assumptions that it diminished as one approached half-filling. Furthermore, the proposed symmetry holds even when boundary effects are accounted for; however, the magnitude of these boundary effects increases with closer proximity to half-filling. Additionally, the magnitude of the sign problem can be markedly reduced through additional fermion-to-boson mappings.

Our framework posits a composite Higgs model where a complex scalar field, comprising a pseudo-Goldstone boson and the would-be eaten Goldstone boson, serves as the domain wall instanton responsible for baryon number violation. This mechanism generates a coherent, periodic electric dipole moment (BP-EDM) for the muon, offering an optimally large signal that is highly accessible at both future muon colliders and existing facilities like the LHC. Moreover, the corresponding tau lepton EDM acts as a remarkably sensitive probe for this phenomenon, provided the tau magnetic moment has been measured with high precision.

"Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations (VPPMs) refer to the process of altering a user's virtual actions within a simulated environment while simultaneously modifying the corresponding physical sensations they experience in the real world. These techniques, which extend beyond standard virtual feedback by acting as advanced versions of haptic correction, significantly influence perceived reality. They facilitate novel interaction paradigms in virtual environments, deepening user engagement. This paper explores the theoretical foundations of VPPMs, outlines their various implementations, and discusses promising future avenues for their development."

We evaluate various methods for integrating new languages—specifically German and Korean—into BigScience's 1.3-billion parameter multilingual pre-trained model. This model originally supports 13 languages. The research examines how different factors influence language adaptation performance and assesses the tradeoffs between computational resources and anticipated results.

Recent observations indicate that protostellar binaries are far more prevalent than previously thought, yet the mechanisms forming these systems remain debated. This study employs high-resolution simulations of turbulent, magnetized gas collapse within a magnetohydrodynamic framework to investigate binary formation. We analyzed the mass distributions of protostars resulting from the direct fragmentation of parent cores of varying masses. Our findings demonstrate that binary fragments are significantly more likely to form when the parent core's mass is low. Specifically, the mass distribution of binary systems born from a single collapsing core follows a power law with a slope of approximately 1.7. While binary frequencies from different parent cores can be combined to create a global mass distribution, we emphasize that this distribution is not a power law. This highlights the critical necessity of accounting for star formation environments and the physical properties of individual collapsing cores to accurately model the overall binary population.

This study introduces the m-arcsinh-based FastICA (m-ar-K-FastICA) algorithm, an enhanced version of FastICA that integrates the mg arcsinh function to increase linearity and minimize skewness. Since standard FastICA is sensitive to random noise, the proposed method incorporates an MMSE filter and a robust cross-covariance estimator to ensure robustness. Additionally, the new algorithm employs an information maximization approach to resolve the ambiguity inherent in mix-covariance estimators. Simulation results indicate that m-ar-K-Fastica delivers superior performance compared to other algorithms in feature extraction, particularly with noisy and random data. The practical utility of the proposed method was validated through its application to the blind source separation of the Hubble Space Telescope's images of the Crab Nebula.

This paper addresses two primary topics. Initially, we demonstrate that if Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPE) can distinguish non-isomorphic graphs within a certain fragment of graph duality, then the bounded-degree extended polynomial calculus (EPC) achieves a completeness result regarding completeness for some k for that same fragment. Additionally, we examine a class of first-order sentences involving k-stars and establish that the order complexity of these sentences correlates with the refutation proof complexity of corresponding first-order axioms within the bounded-degree EPC. Specifically, we establish that the refutation length of these axioms is exponentially small in case CPE requires an exponential number of variables to distinguish certain structures, or exponentially long in case CPE requires a superpolynomial number of variables to do so.

The concept of a concept of $C$-covers for modules was initially introduced by O. A. Soleimanian et al., followed by generalizations to ring covers by the same authors in second paper. In this work, we examine the covering number for unital associative rings, where a cover is defined as any univalent extension of a ring that shares the identical radical. By determining the concepts of $H$-products for modules and a corresponding ring term within our analysis, we establish sufficient requirements to ensure the existence of covering numbers for modules and rings, respectively, with several theorems detailing these concepts.

Social media generates content at an overwhelming rate, making it difficult for users to distinguish accurate information from falsehoods. While fact-checking is essential, traditional expert-led reporting is often slow, costly, and unable to keep pace with the deluge of new content. To address these limitations, this paper introduces an automated verification system that leverages knowledge graphs and graph neural networks. We evaluate a novel enhanced graph neural network architecture against existing state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating increased accuracy. Furthermore, we analyze the influence of various node features and explore how different graph structural encodings perform within the verification process.

The abundance of real-time, unstructured text flowing through social platforms presents a significant opportunity for rapidly identifying and categorizing emerging events, a task with wide-ranging applications in security, public health, and the media. However, constructing event detection systems that are both accurate and adaptable to new domains remains a persistent challenge. To address this, we introduce a deep learning framework designed specifically for event detection in live social streams. This architecture employs recurrent neural networks augmented with an attention mechanism to automatically extract event attributes directly from textual data. Additionally, we developed multi-task learning modules to concurrently predict overlapping event phases and associated hashtags, thereby refining attribute identification and boosting overall performance. Evaluated on two large-scale, real-world datasets, a novel attribute prediction model based on this framework outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches.

This work demonstrates that the weighted skew-spectrum serves as a potent instrument for analyzing cosmic structures, constraining parameters, and testing theoretical models. We detailed the cases for both continuous and discrete data, with specific application to the skew-spectrum of the matter distribution. Results indicate that, in a discrete data framework, the skew-spectrum of the luminosity redshift distribution—when corrected for various biases such as galaxy bias, binning issues, redshift-space distortions, and photometric noise—faithfully reproduces the signal from the original continuous matter skew-spectrum. Applying this method to an eight-bin discrete simulation of the lensing redshift skew-spectrum successfully mirrored the eight-binned continuous matter input. Furthermore, incorporating a galaxy selection function introduces only negligible alterations to the skew-spectrum. Ultimately, given current galaxy survey capabilities, the number of independent skew-spectrum data points derivable from the lensing redshift is vastly superior to that obtainable from other probe types, positioning it as an area ripe for further investigation.

By viewing adversarial training within the probabilistic framework of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs), our research demonstrates a unification of two prevalent adverserial training strategies. This perspective not only clarifies the theoretical rationale behind key adversarial training hyperparameters but also facilitates their more effective tuning. Building on this theory, we propose an innovative method that incorporates gradient uncertainty into the loss function to minimize the model's worst-case error. Experiments across various benchmark datasets and network architectures reveal that this proposed loss function rationally explains standard practices in adversarial training and surpasses current adversarial methods in performance.

The COVID-19 pandemic and the misinformation it spawned have caused widespread panic, making the rapid detection of online emerging rumors a critical challenge. While existing detection approaches typically depend on analyzing content semantics or network structures, this study introduces a semantic-aware graph neural network (GNN) tailored specifically for detecting online rumors. This architecture incorporates a semantics-aware self-attention mechanism to refine node embeddings within the rumor propagation graph, effectively capturing contextual nuances that standard methods might overlook. Additionally, it employs a propagation-aware subgraph sampling strategy to mitigate class imbalance issues inherent in early-stage rumor detection. Validated using the first publicly available dataset of Chinese rumor reports from Weibo, the research demonstrates that the proposed system outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and computational efficiency.

Classifying remote sensing pixels is a critical step in interpreting hyperspectral imagery. While techniques like Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) are commonly used to reduce image dimensionality, there is currently no consensus on selecting the optimal number of principal components or discriminative features. This study evaluates various dimensionality reduction approaches to identify conditions that maximize classification performance. We conducted an extensive experimental analysis on six publicly available hyperspectral datasets, testing the inclusion of features at multiple levels. Our results indicate that a higher compression ratio is preferable for accurate classification, suggesting these methods should be fully maximal. Furthermore, linear methods prove more effective than non-linear alternatives. Finally, accuracy is significantly sensitive to the feature count; therefore, we propose a strategy to determine the ideal number of features rather than arbitrarily selecting them.

The recent discovery known as the "linear neural network hypothesis" or "sparse algorithmic hypothesis" suggests that even highly over-parameterized deep models can be reduced to sparse counterparts that achieve equivalent accuracy. This paper re-examines sparse subnetworks within over-parameterized structures, specifically investigating their general performance and distribution. We find a direct relationship between the test accuracy of these sparse models and the degree of over-parameterization in the original parent network. Furthermore, our results show that the conductance eigenvalues of regularized graph-cut-based tickets follow a regular pattern, often approximated by simple analytical forms. These theoretical insights are substantiated through empirical data from computer vision tasks, using various convolutional architectures such as ResNet, VGG, and Inception.

This study introduces ProCS-2.0, an enhanced tool designed to predict protein backbone amide proton chemical shifts from NMR spectra. The program operates by automatically scanning raw NMR data to detect all crosspeaks, filtering out noise and artifacts through multiple criteria, and then calculating the differences between amide and methyl group chemical shifts to generate the final predictions. When evaluated on a test set of 100 proteins, the software achieved a mean unsigned error (MUE) of 0.37 ppm. Its performance exhibited a strong linear correlation with that of previous state-of-the-art programs, yielding a correlation coefficient (r) of 0.94, while simultaneously demonstrating improved results on specific datasets. Due to its robust reliability and user-friendly design, ProCS-2.0 presents itself as a highly effective resource for structural biologists seeking to map random peptide chemical shifts from experimental NMR files.

The loss function is central to deep neural network (DNN) training for supervised tasks like classification. While cross-entropy remains the standard choice, recent research has explored alternatives. This work offers a theoretical analysis of various entropy-based loss functions for network classification and regression using the lens of effective post-processing. Our findings indicate that these different loss choices primarily alter the position of the decision boundary within effective post-processing mechanisms. Specifically:
*   **General Post-processing Indicator**: The authors define a signpost indicating which entropy losses yield equivalent results regarding the classification outcome.
*   **Logistic Regression Context**: The analysis determines the specific entropy loss equivalent to using cross-entropy in traditional logistic regression.
*   **Highly Nonlinear Networks**: For systems featuring highly nonlinear activations, the study establishes sufficient conditions under a probabilistic framework. This probabilistic model assumes the effective postprocessing relies on a linear activation layer followed by a nearest-nearest neighbor search. It demonstrates that for such non-linear networks, the use of logistic loss functions can yield superior classification performance compared to cross-entropy variants.

Investigating correlated electron systems demands accurate handling of multi-leg correlations. While parquet theory offers a rigorous framework accounting for all such interactions, its original implementation is too computation-heavy for systems with multiple bands. We introduce a bandsimplified parquet formalism designed specifically for two-band models, defined by four distinct scattering channels. We demonstrate the validity and computational efficiency of this approach by simultaneously deriving self-energies and one- and four-vertex functions for a two-band Hubbard model on a square lattice. When benchmarked against quantum Monte Carlo results on the same model, our formalism shows strong agreement. Furthermore, we explore the phase diagrams of the model, identifying characteristic features like pseudogap regions and transition points between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic ordered states.

The phase transition from a semimetal to an excitonic insulator is signaled by the opening of an energy gap and the accumulation of excitons near Fermi surfaces. In this study, we analyze this semimetal-to-excitonic-insulator transition within doped graphene subjected to a magnetic field. Our analysis reveals that the transition in this system is primarily driven by the interaction between Landau levels and the formation of bound electron-hole pairs. We calculated the self-consistent gap equation based on this model and used it to determine critical doping concentrations. Furthermore, we examine how magnetic fields influence both the transition doping level and the magnitude of the energy gap.

Recent research into automated textual emotion detection has largely concentrated on supporting the generation of empathetic responses in chatbots and safety monitoring platforms. However, a significant gap remains regarding which specific emotions most effectively enhance response rates in contexts involving phone-based interactions. To address this, the study presents a novel framework evaluating emotions detected via spoken language.

This study reports on the investigation of dopant-induced superconductivity in the Bi$_2$Se$_3$ doped topological insulator, a material that exhibits a narrow, tunable gap. Using a combination of scanning tunneling microscopy and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we offer a comprehensive analysis of its electronic structure. Our findings reveal that the superconducting state is of the n-type, dopant-induced s-wave variety, which coexists with the small natively formed topological gap. We propose that simultaneously engineering a larger topological gap and inducing stronger superconducting order parameters could serve as an effective strategy to enhance topological superconducting properties.

Active learning methodologies aim to optimize labeling efficiency by identifying the most informative data points for human annotation. Predominant approaches in this field employ either uncertainty or model correction strategies to determine sampling orders. Conversely, our study introduces a novel framework leveraging local density and diversity to achieve an equilibrium between exploration and exploitation. The similarity between predicted classes guides the uncertainty calculation to enhance the selection of high-value samples. Furthermore, the label prediction reliability is increased through a similarity-based correction approach grounded in labeled instance features. Empirical results across three public datasets for image classification demonstrate that the proposed method significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques, particularly under constrained annotation budgets.

This study introduces a novel metric known as loudness complexity to evaluate how dynamic and rhythmic variation in musical intensity influences the emotional character of a piece. This dimension is categorized as "intensity" within the Musical Emotional Geometry (MEG) framework, a model that relates song characteristics to their potential emotional profiles. Our analysis, which examined over 100,000 tracks from the Million Song Dataset, focused on specific acoustic features, such as loudness complexity, to explore trends across the decades. Results indicate that while the average song's loudness has grown more complex since the 1960s, these features have also shifted in their correlation with emotional attributes. Specifically, songs with higher intensity variation are now linked to a more distinct emotional character, whereas music with less complex dynamics tends to evoke emotions that are less differentiated from one another. Consequently, recategorizing songs based on our proposed loudness complexity framework reveals updated emotional profiles that differ meaningfully from previous classifications.

We examine a stochastic process beginning with one number in a block. At each step, a new number either forms a fresh block alone or adds to an existing block with probability proportional to that block's current size. Dividing the total timeline into $n$ discrete time points yields a permutation of $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ at the end, defined by the order in which numbers were introduced. We analyze various random structures associated with the resulting partition, specifically exploring their limits as $n$ grows large.

A dominant approach to reward learning relies on humans providing preferences through comparisons, which is often more practical than explicitly defining reward functions. Nevertheless, this method demands a high number of interactions to converge effectively. We propose a novel paradigm that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) as the forerunner for the actual reward policy, allowing preference data to be collected from "simulated human" LLM agents instead of true people. Because such policy-level LLMs are easier to calibrate and align with values than raw reward policies, this strategy facilitates the gathering of high-quality preference data. We introduce a specific training framework that refines preference-generating LLMs by having them engage in multi-turn conversations, enabling them to mimic sophisticated human judgment often found in experienced tutors rather than inconsistent first-year students. Experiments conducted on reward scenarios for both game playing and writing tasks demonstrate that our proposed method achieves strong performance, despite deriving preferences solely from single-preference interactions from the LLM preference models.

This work investigates the dynamics of ideal 2D fluid points where density variations occur, specifically focusing on the emergence of singularities known as "vortex points." These are isolated regions of zero vorticity embedded within areas of non-zero vorticity, analogous to topological defects in Kosterlitz-Thory theory. Our research centers on the special subclass of these points that maintain a singularity in the velocity field, referred to as "pointed vortex loops." We demonstrate the existence of such structures through a simple ideal fluid model and analyze their behavior using the 2D Euler equations, a task facilitated by the availability of explicit analytical solutions. By integrating this theoretical framework with computational results, we reveal the points' volatility and confirm the points' capacity to persist for extended durations. Ultimately, our findings suggest that these entities may serve as building blocks in the complex evolution of 2D vortex topology.

This work demonstrates that the Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting (AIPW) estimator for average treatment effects possesses dual properties: it is not only a minimum variance estimator within a specific class but also enjoys semi-additivity. Similarly, the nonparametric AIPW (nAIPW) estimator exhibits these traits. These findings provide rigorous justification for the widely used practice of employing machine learning to fit AIPW estimators. The discussion further extends to scenarios involving unobserved confounding, adapting previous theorems to this context. A pivotal byproduct of extending these results is a novel, simple theorem establishing the consistency of the two-stage least means estimator for causal effects in populations with unmeasured confounders.

Particle physics experiments have indicated a potential violation of lepton flavor universality, suggesting the need to investigate new phenomena beyond the Standard Model. As a key process in this inquiry, we present a measurement of the $J/\psi \to \pi^+ \pi^- \tau^+ \tau^-$ decay, which allows for the determination of branching fractions involving tau leptons. This study introduces a new, fully coupled atmospheric circulation model designed to simulate long-term dynamics on rotating spheres, specifically targeting non-zonal flow regimes to advance our understanding of atmospheric science. The model's capacity to replicate cyclogenesis—relying critically on a latitudinal temperature contrast and the rotation rate—is evaluated through visualization of flow patterns and statistical metrics like zonally averaged kinetic energy. We contrast these simulated states with the known non-zonal asymptotic flow identified by Ioannou et al. (2017), demonstrating that the model successfully reproduces similar kinetic energy signatures and kinetic energy dissipation rates as a function of the rotational Omega number.

Modelling extreme values is typically approached through inductive frameworks based on univariate extreme value theory. A key feature of this approach is the use of threshold-invariant parameters, which allow researchers to focus on high thresholds without needing a precise definition. In this study, we introduce a direct method grounded in multivariate elliptical copulas to model the joint distribution of rare events. This proposal utilizes the concepts of relative extremum and the upper M-dependence structure. We demonstrate, with specific elliptical examples, the feasibility of estimating parameters for both the shape parameter $\gamma$ and the $M$-dependence count. We further develop an elliptical family tailored for $U$-closed upper M-extremum distributions, enabling the estimation of $\gamma$-specific parameters. This advancement permits a more accurate determination of $\gamma$ by reducing reliance on $D$, the count of variables, thereby minimizing the needed sample size. We illustrate these methods using a U-shaped distribution and provide an epidemiological application of this procedure.

This paper investigates the resilience of offline reinforcement learning (RL) agents against adversarial data poisoning. We examine a scenario in offline RL where an adversary modifies an arbitrary $\varepsilon$ fraction of the data within an environment trajectory. The central research question is determining the minimum modification threshold ($\varepsilon$) capable of degrading the performance of the optimal policy below a certain level $\delta$. By modeling the reward and transition functions as being represented by linear operators, the authors derive performance bounds, revealing that the optimal policy is best approximated by linear function of the perturbed reward and square-root-attenuated perturbed transition models. The study identifies that the most damaging adversarial strategy involves modifying rewards, specifically by flipping their signs. Empirical evaluations across the CliffWalking task and a disease progression model demonstrate the effectiveness of these attacks. Notably, the attacks succeed even when the adversary modifies up to 50% of the tuples in substantial problems, confirming the vulnerability of standard RL methods. These results motivate the development of robust offline RL techniques, which the authors address in a subsequent section.

This paper establishes logarithmic convexity as a consequence of an observability estimate at a critical time step for 1-D hyperbolic diffusion systems with dynamic boundary conditions. Based on this result, it proves the exact and impulse controllability of the heat equation under the same conditions, demonstrating how impulse controllability arises from achieving critical-time exact controllability.

Although detecting out-of-distribution (ODD) samples is crucial for real-world applications, many existing methods fail to generalize effectively when encountering unknown types of shift (UOS). Current research typically categorizes ODD detection into two strategies: intrinsic, which relies on data characteristics, and extrinsic, which utilizes an external model. This study introduces a novel extrinsic approach called ENN (Exponential Smoothing-based Nearest Neighbors), designed to extract insights from a Nearest Neighbors classifier regarding data distribution. Our core hypothesis posits that UOS examples exhibit distinct patterns in their distance metrics compared to in-distribution data. Specifically, we observe that nearest neighbors for UOS instances tend to be farther away and more dispersed than those for in-distribution examples. Consequently, we apply an exponential smoothing technique to the distance distribution of a Nearest Neighbors classifier to identify significant gaps, effectively distinguishing intrinsic from extrinsic features. Experimental results demonstrate that enNN surpasses existing benchmarks across various outdoor domains, achieving near-perfect scores in class activation diagram tests and demonstrating robustness and simplicity in handling unseen domain challenges.

The most promising route for controlling artificial molecular motors appears to be the modulation of reaction barriers via electric currents. Although recent progress has been made in understanding how electrons couple to vibrations and reactions within single-molecule junctions, existing data are scarce on how this coupling influences the conformational changes essential to molecular motors. This study employs a combination of transition state theory and Kramers' rate theory to calculate the conformational switching rates of a standard V-shaped motor. Our findings suggest that a current flowing through a rotor–substrate junction can accelerate or decelerate the motor's rotation, with magnitude effects hinging on the rotor's height and the conduction pathway's resistance. Furthermore, we have identified specific conditions under which the conformational reorientation occurs elastically, a scenario in which applied current exerts minimal influence on the switching rate.

Origin semantics for transducers were formalized in the 1990s within category theory but have seen limited application compared to classical models. To date, no self-luminous exoplanet has been confirmed, though gaseous giant GJ 229B, discovered over three decades ago, has long held that title. Recent, high-precision spectroscopic atmospheric models successfully characterize the planet's structure and dynamics. Despite these advances, its classification as the solar system's coldest extended body remains a point of contention. This study applies the latest retrieval algorithms to a broad spectrum of observed spectral data to refine estimates of the planet's mass and radius while modeling diverse cloud scenarios. The analysis yields a best-fit effective temperature ($T_{\rm eff}$) of 253 K and a mass ($M_{\rm p}$) of 16.6 Jupiter masses ($M_{\rm J}$), with results showing minimal sensitivity to cloud opacity assumptions. These findings indicate that the planet is cooling significantly slower than previously thought, suggesting a sluggish convection speed of 0.005 cm s$^{-1}$. Such a state of thermal convection implies an extended, super-adiabatic convective zone approximately 10$^5$ km thick. These characteristics suggest GJ 229B possesses a heavy-element core of roughly 100 Earth masses ($M_{\odot}$) within an envelope dominated by molecular hydrogen and helium. Ultimately, these results offer critical insights for upcoming, high-fidelity data expected from the JWST era.

To investigate potential exotic configurations, we performed global fits of lattice QCD correlation functions, focusing on the $J^{PC}=0^{--}$ channel within the mass range below 2 GeV. Our analysis, which involved fitting these functions to identify any non-conventional states, yielded a unique best-fit result with acceptable statistical consistency across multiple $\chi^2$ variations; however, this uniqueness is constrained, as alternative fit configurations also explain the data adequately. This ambiguity implies that below 2 GeV, a $0^{--}$ exotic state either does not exist or possesses extremely small coupling to quark-antiquark ($q\bar{q}$) meson pairs. Consequently, we propose that the observed correlation can equally be described by the interference of scalar ($J^{PC}=0^{++}$) and pseudoscalar ($J^{PC}=0^{-+}$) standard $q\bar{q}$ mesons.

A principal objective of the LHCb collaboration, which operates at the Large Hadron Collider, is to determine the CKM unitarity triangle, specifically the mixing-induced $C\!P$-violating phase angle $\phi_{s}$ and the mass difference parameter $x_{s} \equiv \Gamma_{s}^{d}/\Delta m_{s}$ in flavor physics. This region involves the oscillations of neutral bottom baryons into their antiparticles, a phenomenon governed by the mass difference $\Delta m_{s}$. LHCb has recently achieved significant progress in observing these phenomena in $\Lambda_{b}^{0}$ and $\overline{\Lambda}_{b}^{0}$ decays to final states containing two $D^{(-)}$ mesons and one soft lepton, as well as in three-body decays involving $D^{*(-)}$ mesons. This article provides a current overview of these measurement efforts, highlighting recent advancements and future perspectives for determining these fundamental parameters with higher precision.

Airborne viruses are primarily disseminated through infected individuals' exhalations, often while they engage in face-to-face interactions. To assess the probability of airborne viral transmission in confined areas, we must examine the combined effects of respiratory airflow, airborne viral transport, and inhaled viral dose. This study presents a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) analysis of airflow patterns generated by two individuals conversing, alongside the turbulent dispersion of particulate matter emitted by an infectious person. The study also quantifies the viral dose received by a susceptible person based on specific variables: emission rate of viruses, concentration of airborne viruses, concentration of particulate matter, and inhalation rate. These calculations are performed to determine transmission risk. The study concludes by offering risk estimations for various conversational settings and proposing mitigation strategies to prevent the spread of airborne infections.

The shell-model analysis of $\beta$-decay properties for the N=28 neutron shell closure, utilizing the standard $fp$-shell model space, demonstrates that shell-model models effectively reproduce the observed $ft$ values and $\beta$-branching ratios within this region. The authors derive $Q_{\beta}$ values from these calculated structural properties and compare them with experimental data or limits where necessary; the resulting agreement with measured $Q_{\beta}$ offers robust support for the adequacy of the $fp$-shell model space in this mass region.

Double-sided auctions, prevalent in financial markets, facilitate matching supply and demand for goods or services. While standard research often limits analysis to single-unit trades, many real-world scenarios involve multiple quantities. This study investigates double-sided auction double-matchings for multiple-unit trades, formulating the matching process as a linear programming problem to optimize for the total value of matched trades. By employing the Open Source linear solver CBC, we address this problem practically. Our numerical experiments, grounded in financial data, analyze the running times of various matching algorithms and their result qualities. We also propose an iterative algorithm designed to enhance solution values, offering solutions that are both computationally efficient and of high quality.

We examine $F$-wave bottom mesons within the heavy quark effective framework, employing the established method of analysis. Our study encompasses the spin–spin couplings, the masses of spin–spin splitting, and the masses themselves for these states. Using a set of empirical constraints, we determine a total of thirteen effective parameters. With this fitted model in place, we predict physical properties for the remaining members. We provide the predictive mass formulae and present our mass predictions in tabulated format, comparing them with existing experimental data and theoretical models. Finally, our tables also list the theoretical uncertainties and potential errors.

This study examines the nonexpansive lines that arise within a setting of examples, specifically focusing on the periodic configuration space $\mathbb{A}^{\mathbb{C}}$, where $\mathbb{C}$ represents the set of complex numbers and $\mathbb{A}$ signifies a finite set. These lines are demonstrated through a technique utilizing the theory of holomorphic motion.

The rise of data-driven systems has generated a surge in research for modeling them using machine learning techniques. However, existing literature largely ignores the integration of physical knowledge into this modeling framework. To address this gap, we propose a "learning-based system identification" framework that meets rigorous passivity constraints. The framework begins by defining a data-driven series expansion for the input-output behavior of series-passive systems, followed by the derivation of a convex optimization algorithm capable of estimating system parameters while guaranteeing passivity. Series expansions are found effective because the learning process can focus exclusively on a modest set of relevant basis functions embedded with physical insights, rather than voluminous data-driven functions. Additionally, the framework is extended to handle systems influenced by random noise. Through simulations involving both lossless and strictly positive real systems—encompassing both series and parallel models— the framework's effectiveness is demonstrated.

Large-scale opening databases present significant challenges for users seeking relevant information, particularly base knowledge for refining game openings. By leveraging ChessVG data, this paper constructs an extensive relatedness network for openings, demonstrating that chess theories align closely with the structure of a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST). We propose an interactive web tool that helps players rapidly grasp this theoretical structure and refine their opening strategies. Users can explore this MST through various visual formats, while also receiving highly recommended moves at specific points. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that AI models exhibit strong adherence to established chess theories.

This study investigates key observational features of millisecond pulsars—including magnetic field strength, spin duration, and mass—in order to examine potential accretion-driven formation mechanisms. We focus on a specific subset of millisecond pulsars characterized by magnetic fields weaker than $10^{-8}$ Gauss and spin periods shorter than 10 milliseconds, conditions that signal a white dwarf accretion origin. By modeling the evolution of these pulsars during active white dwarf accretion, we simulate a sample of 1000 objects to derive key distribution profiles for magnetic field, spin period, and mass. We then compare these synthetic distributions against real observational data to constrain global parameters governing the formation and post-accretion evolution of millisecond pulsars. The analysis yields a white dwarf mass range of $0.5$–$1.0$ solar masses and an initial rotational velocity for the accreting star of $10^{-4}$–$10^{-3}$ solar rotations per second. Furthermore, we investigate how the spin-down rate of an accreting white dwarf is influenced by magnetic field strength and estimate the magnitude of magnetic braking effects in this context.

This work examines the impact of dissipipation on the emergence of nonlocal constants of motion within mechanical systems. Our findings demonstrate that for a dissipative system to admit a nonlocal constant of motion, the associated mechanical system must possess specific estimates ensuring bounded solution growth over time. Additionally, we establish that certain nonlocal constants of motion, such as the energy of the Abelian mechanical system and specific magnetic variants, cannot exist in dissipative systems. Furthermore, we prove that any nonlocal constant of motion defined as an integral of a variational integral must arise from a conservative system rather than one undergoing any form of dissipation. These proofs employ techniques from geometric control theory, notably the theory of Chaterian semigroups and the analysis of geodesic flows.

This paper describes the implementation of 3D model retrieval via air-doodling in a VR setting using hand gestures. The system leverages Point-SLAM for navigation and employs a neural network based on PointNet++ to perform the shape completion task. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the impact of various factors on the recovery process, including different VR headsets, point cloud sampling rates, and network architectures. Additionally, an ablation study investigates how network design influences performance when trained on public datasets versus data collected from actual user interactions.

Highly eccentric orbits around stars cause exoplanets to experience extreme fluctuations in received insolation, driving them through periastron in a brief window while spent long durations at apastron. Such orbital dynamics are anticipated to significantly influence atmospheric circulation and surface conditions. This study investigates the atmospheric response of an Earth-like body on an eccentric path utilizing a 2-D, hydrostatic, axisymmetric, and hemispheric-resolving climate model. We find that while global mean surface temperatures track the effective stellar flux, local anomalies emerge, particularly in the cold traps located at the apastron sub-stellar point. Furthermore, the timing of the periastron passage dictates the phase lag of seasonal cycles, influencing how seasonal variability compares between planets receiving identical average light levels. Although heat redistribution remains efficient, a distinct "periastron wind" arises, driven by equator-to-pole flows in the subsolar region as the planet approaches its star, superimposed on standard apastron winter and periastron summer circulations.

This study examines the relativistic gravitational collapse of a barotropic perfect fluid, where the equation of state is expressed as $p=p(\rho)$, within the framework of the 1+1+1 Misner-Changina-Zakharov formalism. Because the field equations constitute a system of quasi-linear partial differential equations (PDEs) involving four independent variables and four unknown dependent variables, specific constraints on the equation of state are essential for the PDEs to remain compatible. By applying a determinant-based method to enforce this compatibility, the authors derive a necessary condition that aligns with the Barrabes-Israel formalism. They subsequently demonstrate that the derived condition is both adequate and correct for the optical singularity formation scenarios in a perfect fluid containing radiation and/or heat-conducting components. Furthermore, for a collapsing fluid obeying the equation of state $\rho=3p$, the authors present the complete, analytically exact solution to the PDEs. They demonstrate that the location and nature of the resulting optical singularity are dictated by the arbitrary1-f-dimensional space-like functions $f^i(x^j)$ appearing in the solution set.

We establish that extensions to the extremality condition for generic $D=5$ asymptotically flat electrically charged black holes and holes can be systematically mapped by analyzing the corresponding adjustments in an associated extremality parameter for scalar-variant versions of that same configuration. Building upon our prior work in reinforcement learning for motor learning, this paper introduces a novel approach to constructing virtual anatomical models. Our method utilizes reinforcement learning to fine-tune a random set of end-effect drives within a multi-agent system, targeting the collective objective of maximizing the coherence of achieved poses relative to a defined coherent pose distribution. Our findings demonstrate that this proposed model generation technique surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, producing more anatomically realistic results.

We extend the three-dimensional Poincaré algebra to incorporate a colour symmetry factor, creating an associated graded algebra. This framework allows for both the formulation of coloured three-dimensional Poincaré gravity and a deeper exploration of expanded massive or massless free particle models. Furthermore, the mechanics governing motion for two coloured massless particles are derived and applied to construct a novel field theory of coloured three-dimensional gravity.

We introduce an enhanced version of the original MemoNav framework, designed to address first-person multi-goal within a single image-based dataset. The system constructs a graph representing the scene by learning both topological and metric relationships between images, employing a novel metric regression module that integrates visual comparisons with memory-derived cues for superior accuracy. By allowing the navigation network to refer back to the STM alongside the primary memory, STM acts as a dynamic roadblock filter and facilitates more direct path planning. We investigate how operators evolve in systems exhibiting Lie symmetry. In the idealized limit of infinite system dimensions, the complexity of an operator's biorthogonal state increases linearly with time. This study focuses on generators belonging to the algebra related to the given system and demonstrates that their operator spread can be derived exactly using the fractional Calogero-Bargmann method. The analysis reveals distinct, universal features regarding how these operators compactify in both real and internal spatial directions. Furthermore, we illustrate that our methodology extends to representative models, enabling the exploration of systems where numerical approximations are insufficient.

The structural nature of the Hoyle state has long been a subject of debate, pitting a clusterized model against a pure bosonic $\alpha$-condensate interpretation. A key experimental handle for distinguishing between these possibilities is the direct-to-total decay ratio into three alpha particles ($\alpha\alpha\alpha$), as this metric constrains the wave function at coalescence points. This study presents a first measurement of this ratio within the A=12 mass region, specifically determining the value for the first $0^+$ state in the $^{12}$Be isotope. By performing a direct comparison with established data for the canonical $^{12}$C Hoyle state, our results indicate that the $^{12}$Be state exhibits a significantly lower three-alpha decay probability. This finding confirms the conclusion drawn previously for $^{12}$Be's structure, showing it differs markedly from the classic $\alpha$-condensate behavior observed in $^{12}$C.

Dynamic fracture in 2D brittle materials is typically studied using finite element simulations, which offer clear insights into complex phenomena like crack oscillation. However, this study introduces an analytical model derived from the dynamics of bonds to key variables governing dynamic fracture, based on the assumption that a propagating crack can be represented as a line with energy associated with bond breaking in the wake. High-speed cracks exhibit velocity-dependent oscillatory instability, a feature captured effectively by this model. Specifically, it determines the lower velocity threshold for oscillation onset and defines the stability boundaries in the parameter space of inertial effects versus bond-breaking energy release rates. The stability analysis reveals a transition from stability regions defined by Bond Energy and Inertial effects at low velocities to those determined by Bond Energy and Maximum Available Energy Release Rate ($\sigma_{max}$) at high velocities.

This study investigates spin-triplet superconductivity within a 1D electron gas situated on the surface of a cubic crystal, subjected to a Zeeman magnetic field aligned with the quantization axis. The analysis reveals that Rashba spin-orbit coupling must be present to establish a finite gap on the Fermi sphere; notably, this effect is observable even when the field is applied along the $z$-axis. The resulting gap profile follows an isotropic form, $|\Delta(\mathbf{k})| = |\Delta_0|$, where the order parameter $\Delta_0$ exhibits a sign ambiguity. Specifically, the ratio between the major ($\Delta_{\text{maj}}$) and minor ($\Delta_{\text{min}}$) components of the gap defines this sign, as does the orientation relative to the Rashba momentum $\mathbf{k}_{\mathrm{R}}$. At fixed Fermi energy and Zeeman strength, there exists a continuous range of allowed $k_{\mathrm{R}}$ values. Furthermore, applying a transverse Zeeman field splits this $k_{\mathrm{R}}$ continuum into two distinct sectors corresponding to opposite spin-orbit masses. The text concludes by outlining the conditions under which the sign of the gap switches and estimating the resulting critical magnetic field.

The rise of tabular data has led to increased interest in claim verification within this domain. To address scenarios lacking complete evidence, particularly in cases where partial support exists, the authors introduce two specific sub-tasks: Tabular Partially Supported Claims Verification (TopsVC) and TopsVnF. The proposed dataset, which is the first large-scale collection designed for this purpose, contains over 20,000 claims extracted from academic papers and news articles involving more than 770,000 cells across various tables found online. The dataset size encompasses more than seven hundred thousand cell entries. The authors also present two models, which are designed for TPOSVC and TPOSVCnN, which are based on two key principles: ensuring consistency between claims and supporting tables, and extracting and cross-referencing supporting evidence from unconnected tables found in source documents.

This investigation explores the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics. We survey prominent rationales commonly cited in literature advocating for complex formalism while introducing additional persuasive arguments. This concise study seeks to reinforce the deep, intrinsic significance of complex numbers in the theoretical framework of Quantum Mechanics.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a simple, connected, and undirected graph, and suppose $S \subseteq V$ is an ordered set where each vertex is assigned either a natural number or the symbol $\infty$ acting as their distance to elements in $S$. This setup defines an *L-labeling* for $G$ if, for every pair of distinct vertices, the difference in their assigned numerical distances (or difference between distance and infinity) is non-zero. The *minimum k-L-labeling* refers to an L-assignment where the sum of degrees for any $k$ is minimized, and the *k-resolving number*, denoted $rd_k(G)$, represents the smallest possible dimension $k$ that allows a valid k-L-labeling to exist. When $k=|V|-1$, this framework generalizes the conventional idea of an ordered resolving set and metric dimension; under these conditions, the definitions of $r_1(G)$ and traditional dimension align. We also compare our findings with an integrable model—the completely resonant case—highlighting the contrast in results.

The paper introduces a fresh connection between two well-established algorithms for producing uniform spanning trees (USTs): Fill's random walk approach and Wilson's algorithm. The study establishes that the path length produced by Fill's method when USTs are created on simple graphs follows a geometric distribution with a mean of $\log n$. Building on this finding, the authors demonstrate a result in the context of random graphs: the branch length of a tree rooted at a randomly selected node in $G_{n,p}$ converges to a Weibull distribution. Furthermore, the authors extend their analysis to a class of graphs exhibiting "$\log$-trapping," showing that the branch length at the root follows a compound Weibull distribution. The final section addresses the path length at the root of a tree formed in $G_{n,p}$ when the probability $p$ is sufficiently high, finding that it approaches a Poisson distribution.

This paper introduces the MusicDD-Dataset, a new resource designed to enhance modal disentanglement in music. The dataset comprises three distinct modalities: musical scores, audio, and rendered three-dimensional models. We provide implementation details for our music generation pipeline and the stochastic variation of musical scores. Additionally, our paper outlines a neural architecture specifically developed for the stochastic disentanglement of these modalities. Empirical results demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms existing baseline approaches on the MusicDD-Dataset.

A primary challenge in consuming Linked Data involves designing visual and natural language interfaces accessible to non-technical users. This paper explores the potential of distributional semantics models to do so by representing data through "semantic vectors." We introduce a prototype system demonstrating how these models can analyze and investigate Linked Data through natural language queries while also evaluating their performance and limitations.

This study examines the nonlinear Schrödinger equation featuring black solitons, which require the inclusion of dispersion that varies with intensity to ensure stability. While such dispersion necessitates modifying the definition of energy functional derivatives, which in turn impacts the standard application of the standard energy method for stability analysis, this work successfully demonstrates asymptotic stability for black solitons with small small perturbations using the energy method. Additionally, it is established that such dispersion must have specific sign characteristics.

Although human-in-the-loop visual analytics (VI) is recognized as a superior approach, the term "human-adaptive" is often misused, receiving little scrutiny regarding its core concept. Effective human-adaptive VI should genuinely adjust system behavior based on an understanding of individual users' specific needs, goals, and actions. The original "human-adaptive" framework, proposed by Keim et al. in 2009, provided a comprehensive model of human visual analytics process interaction that remains highly relevant today. This paper re-examines Keim et al.'s model with a focus on modern human-adaptive VI systems, exploring two critical aspects: (1) identifying which components within the model facilitate personalized adaptation and (2) outlining the emerging technical challenges required to fully realize effective human-adaptive VI.

Effective control of thermal profiles within catalytic fixed bed reactors is vital for ensuring process safety and optimizing yields. We present a new methodology to manage temperature distribution by adjusting the inlet fluid mixture ratio in a two-reactant exothermic first-order series reaction system. This study examines a one-dimensional model that accounts for coupled heat and mass transfer dynamics, nonlinear reaction kinetics, and convective heat transfer. The proposed control framework consists of three phases: first, linearizing the system around an operating point and discretizing the resulting partial differential equations; second, formulating and solving an finite-horizon optimal control problem using direct multiple-shooting techniques; and third, regenerating the optimal control policy repeatedly at short intervals to compensate for initial assumptions. The effectiveness of this strategy is validated through simulations comparing control performance with and considering constraints versus a model that ignores them.

Biomolecular condensates form spontaneously within the dense cellular environment when proteins and nucleic acids undergo phase separation into liquid droplets, a process essential for the spatial organization of life forms. Although the physical characteristics of these droplets are reasonably well-documented, the specific molecular drivers responsible for their formation and their interactions with the complex cellular soup remain obscure. This study investigates the phase behavior of multicomponent systems to determine how droplets nucleate and behave inside a molecular mixture. We developed a simplified model comprising three components to simulate protein droplets and a mobile polymer acting as a cellular obstacle course, alongside immobile polymers representing cell debris. Employing self-consistent field theory, we mapped the thermodynamic phase space of this system to analyze component enrichment within the separated droplets and assess phase boundaries relative to binary simplifications. Our results indicate that nucleation occurs via gas-liquid phase separation at polymer concentrations higher than those required for phase coexistence in a two-component scenario, and we observed that droplet composition can deviate markedly from direct projections based solely on two major constituents. These insights offer a new theoretical framework for understanding droplet formation mechanisms and provide crucial parameters for designing experiments to decode the role of proteins and macromolecules in cellular phase separation.

This study investigates the rotation of sunspots and the subsequent evolution of their magnetic fields following flares. Utilizing observations from the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory's Michelson Doppler Imager, we analyzed the pre-flare states of 13 bipolar flux ropes and tracked their post-flare rotations. The study spot's initial rotation was assessed by calculating the mean angular velocities of umbral bright points surrounding the central umbra, assuming a solar rotation rate of 2.70°/day. The analysis revealed an equal split between right- and left-handed rotations in the umbral points, with no evident link to the global solar magnetic field's handedness. Furthermore, unrotched umbral cores were frequently observed. The mean angular velocities of these umbral bright points ranged between 0.04°/day and 0.14°/day, representing a fraction of the solar background rotation. Following a flare event, the magnetic field topology was significantly reconfigured, causing unumbra to fragment into smaller components and acquire new magnetic structures. The post-flare rotation dynamics were assessed by examining the track curvature of umbral bright points. The study concludes that a solar flare does not invariably induce unumbra rotation, although when rotation does occur post-flare, it exhibits increased speed compared to the pre-flare state.

This note introduces and defines the $b$-principle for oriented colored broken submersions (obcs) and demonstrates the existence of such submersions within a specific homotopy category. Furthermore, we establish the $b$-principle for $b$-colored submersions (bcs) derived from our findings. A byproduct of our approach yields a generalization of He's theorem from [1].

This study introduces and evaluates two techniques for pre-conditioning the nonlinear Newton solver in cardiac mechanical problems: the traditional domain decomposition approach and a new method that decomposes the Newton system based on mechanical components. While the traditional method requires spatial separation at every Newton iteration, producing dense sub-systems in nearly incompressible materials, the new strategy organizes decomposition around functional modules of the Newton process, maintaining a problem structure aligned with static solution features and utilizing robust dense-to-sparse preconditioning. Dense sub-system arithmetic is eliminated except during the final convergence stage. Implemented in the finite element software Carmelot, both methods were tested against a single monolithic solver across three problem types—passive stiffness, active contraction, and fiber architecture—across meshes ranging from 100k to over 100 million nodes. Performance was measured by iterations and wall-clock time to reach numerical tolerance. Results indicate the mechanical decomposition method is most efficient for monolithic solvers, whereas domain decomposition offers superior efficiency when compared to alternative strategies requiring only less than ten iterations to converge.

User-generated tagging systems facilitate collaboration across a vast array of items, serving as a form of collective, folksonomy-based classification. Despite the intuitive nature of these systems, the optimal design remains elusive. The primary objective of this work is to systematically analyze tags and their associated activities within the Reddit community. By examining both large-scale, global-scale data as well as context-specific subsets, the study evaluates various aspects of user behavior and tagging patterns to gain deeper insights.

The paper introduces the theoretical framework for bianisotropic acoustic metagratings and demonstrates their application as ultra-wideband phase and amplitude metasurfaces. Although intrinsic acoustic reciprocity imposes specific constraints, the proposed structures achieve a remarkable form of reciprocity bypass, enabling a wide- and full-dual linear polarization states. The validity of this approach is supported by a non-conventional analytical surface impedance and impedance model, formulated specifically to handle scenarios where the impedance and permeability tensors of a metagrating interface are non-symmetric, thereby expanding design possibilities. Furthermore, we explore several promising applications including multi-dual-band ultrasound imaging and beamforming. The study concludes by suggesting potential avenues for further investigation into this emerging field.

This paper investigates the long-term asymptotic behavior of the strong solutions within the 2-D FENE dumbbell model, which incorporates nonlinear effects from finite extensibility. By leveraging the strong solutions established previously by Li, Ding, and Yu (2020), which satisfy initial-boundary value conditions in a bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbf{R}^2$ with the Navier slip boundary condition, we demonstrate that the $L^2$ norm decays following an algebraic inverse square root rate over large time intervals.

This paper addresses the multi-objective optimization of an IAB network featuring integrated access and backhaul. It examines three distinct goals: maximizing the total sum rate, minimizing the count of backhaul links, and reducing overall power consumption. Because simultaneously optimizing these objectives is computationally prohibitive, we introduce a single-link optimization framework. This approach optimizes key parameters—specifically association, scheduling, and power allocation—for individual IAB links sequentially. A key challenge within this framework is the non-convex nature of the objective functions alongside complex constraints, which we resolve by transforming the problems into convex forms using second-order cone constraints and applying the Sequential Linear Programming method for iterative solution. Following the construction of a two-stage, two-objective optimization model for link-level processing, we employ the $\epsilon$-constraint method to handle the resulting multi-objectivity. Finally, we outline the implementation of this algorithm and present the main results in a comparative analysis format.

A primary goal of evolutionary computation (EC) is optimization, a task whose effectiveness hinges on landscape characteristics, which define the problem and dictate how well an algorithm will perform. Since EC techniques are generally problem-agnostic, there is substantial interest in matching specific algorithms to suitable landscape features to optimize performance. This paper examines a multi-objective binary classification problem, analyzing the relationship between a dataset's characteristics and the efficacy of evolutionary methods for its classification. We propose the use of information theory to measure a landscape's difficulty and demonstrate that multi-objective classifiers can be effectively evolved using tournament selection with or without a two-tournament variation, but struggle when paired with the Rank selection operator. These findings suggest that evolutionary algorithm design must be problem-specific, as a one-size-fits-all methodology may not always yield successful outcomes.

We investigate electromagnetic scenarios involving point particles with finite charge and current density. By reformulating Lagrangian (3+1)-D dynamics into a first-order variational problem, the resulting field equations derived are Maxwell's equations coupled with the equations for charge distribution. These solutions admit an analytically tractable representation using Laplace transforms, which also facilitates verifying that they satisfy the continuity equation. Furthermore, this framework enables the calculation of self-forces for various motion types; for example, it reveals that a purely self-propelled particle experiencing constant velocity encounters no net self-force, whereas a particle oscillating around a track generates a self-force that vanishes only when average radiation reaction over an oscillation cycle balances the applied external radiation reaction over the same period.

Although significant advancements have been made in various domains, most reinforcement learning approaches fail to address the characteristics typically found in real-world open environments, particularly the necessity for continual learning. Consequently, the reinforcement learning field has seen relatively little research into open-world settings. To bridge this gap, we introduce the concept of continual reinforcement learning within a dynamic, transferable task setting, structured as a Markov decision process. By drawing inspiration from the success of semantic semantic segmentation in computer vision, we adapt these features to help distinguish task identities and reduce negative transfer. We then outline a strategy for establishing performance baselines across both semi-supervised and unsupervised classifications. Finally, we present a comprehensive suite of benchmarks designed to facilitate future research in this field.

This paper introduces the discovery of compactly supported and non-compactly supported traveling waves for the 2D Euler equation, formulated in an exponentially weighted $L^2$ framework. This setting permits solutions that vanish outside a specific region, distinguishing them from previously known, non-vanishing traveling waves that exist only within Gevrey spaces. Our advanced weighted $L^2$ approach, which establishes the existence of these new classes of solutions, is applicable to a broader spectrum of periodic 2D fluid models. Additionally, the study examines the regularity and asymptotic behavior of these waves and demonstrates the construction of such solutions across diverse vector fields. This framework also enhances and unifies multiple existing methods, including those used by Demouche & Zaki, Alinhac, and the authors of this work.

The COVID-19 pandemic, a highly contagious respiratory illness, prompted governments worldwide to implement social distancing policies aimed at slowing transmission. These measures include mandatory face masks, hand sanitization, quarantine protocols, travel restrictions, and limiting gatherings. To guide effective implementation, it is essential to assess the specific impact of these actions. This study evaluates the contributions of various distancing strategies to COVID-19 mitigation by integrating a Short-Term Memory (STM) neural network with a system of ordinary differential equations (NN-ODEs). We adapt this dual-framework to an SIR epidemiological model representing susceptible, infected, and recovered populations through dedicated neural network units that encode the dynamics dictated by the underlying differential equations. While the neural network captures the nonlinear interactions of the NN-ODE system, the method utilizes just two datasets—specifically, the current number of susceptible and infected individuals—to forecast the impact of social distancing on the epidemic's trajectory.

Regarding subsets of the integers, Freiman's $3k-4$ theorem reveals two primary structural properties when the sumset size is constrained: the set either resides within an arithmetic progression with a dimension no greater than twice its own, or it exhibits a sumset twice the size of the set plus two. This article presents the first non-asymptotic proof of these Freiman theorems, leveraging the combinatorial arithmetic of the related "companion" structures. Concurrently, we introduce a distinct "companion" framework applicable to various metric spaces that unifies and extends established techniques from one-dimensional cases. This generalization allows us to extend several foundational results in additive combinatorics—specifically those by Freiman's, the sumset decomposition of Ruzsa, and arithmetic progression structures—to higher dimensions and other metric contexts.

Medical procedures often rely on diverse forms of multimodal patient data, yet aggregating these datasets for joint training remains difficult due to privacy concerns and logistical barriers. We introduce an original framework for distributed multital dataset pretraining that allows each institution to retain local ownership while still facilitating collaboration. In this system, models remain hosted locally at each university; only lightweight model updates are transmitted for aggregation back to their point of origin. This ensures that raw patient data never leaves its host facility, effectively addressing both the challenges posed by data silos and those related to privacy. The approach is evaluated across three clinical applications—specifically cardiac disease detection, histopathology analysis, and mixed modality inputs—leveraging data from three distinct academic centers. The proposed method achieves performance comparable to central pretraining models trained on all datasets together, confirming that high-quality results are possible without the need to centralize sensitive data.

Assessing the severity of COVID-19 remains essential for effective clinical care, yet current diagnostic methods often rely on scarce and inconsistent resources, leading to delayed decisions. Although existing studies have utilized machine learning with manually extracted features to predict disease severity, these approaches are often labor-intensive and overlook potential patterns within raw imaging data. This study introduces a deep learning framework that leverages residual networks to process original X-ray scans, with a specific focus on severe outcomes. The proposed method utilizes a multi-branch architecture to concurrently maximize semantic representations and retain access to unfocused input images. We evaluated this model using a public dataset containing chest X-rays from 1,473 COVID-19 patients and compared its performance against several established benchmarks, demonstrating superior predictive capabilities.

Discovering new intents from user inputs is a critical capability for natural language understanding (NLU) in dialogue systems. While existing approaches typically depend on supervised learning requiring extensive labeled datasets, they often lack ability to Introduce discovered intents and their associated slot labels efficiently. In this work, we present a structured, unsupervised discovery framework that enables rapid annotation of intent and slot information for new intents. Our methodology employs clustering to isolate candidate intents from unlabeled data, predicts intent states via neural network classifiers, and infers slot values using CRF models. Subsequently, human annotators validate and refine the predicted annotations, a process demonstrated to be significantly more straightforward and faster than annotating intents from scratch. Experimental results demonstrate that our full pipeline successfully identified 38.5% of intents present in a target dataset; notably, when applied to the AllDialog dataset, our system identified over 10,000 additional intents and over 50,000 slot values in just a few hours.

Despite recent significant advancements in the field, Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) still faces the persistent challenge of high false-positive rates. A primary reason for this is class imbalance during training, which stems from numerous negative examples that are far more abundant than positive instances. While prior strategies have attempted to mitigate this imbalance, they often overlook the distinct characteristics of these negative samples. The authors introduce an improved approach by more effectively leveraging negative examples through a two-fold strategy. First, they propose a refined pre-filtering method to eliminate obvious false positives, thereby enhancing the quality of negatives used for model re-weighting. Second, they propose learning a specific embedding for these filtered negatives to guide the model in distinguishing them from actual positive cases. Additionally, the approach integrates a class-balanced contrastive loss function to achieve more equitable feature representation. Empirical results on the COCO dataset demonstrate that this methodology surpasses all existing techniques for improving the accuracy of visual relation detection using negative samples.

This study examines the evolution of weak measurement combined with weak tracing to investigate resource costs. We demonstrate that the correlation resource cost under weak tracing (WTC) exceeds the weak tracing correlation resource cost under weak tracing (WTT) for all considered systems. Furthermore, we find that the quantum correlation resource under weak tracing surpasses the weak tracing-based quantum discord. Additionally, we derive analytical expressions for both the weak tracing-based geometric quantum discord and the correlation resource under weak tracing when applied to two-qubit states.

Understanding social contexts within visual environments is vital for human intelligence, yet current automated systems often lack the depth required to model social interactions effectively. We introduce the Social Relationship Graph (SRG) as a mechanism to represent and refine these interactions. An SRG captures entities, their relationships, and the social contexts they inhabit, with refiners enhancing entity attributes based contextual information. We refine this process through two key operations: (1) *visual reasoning*, which infers the attributes of an entity from its visual characteristics and relational data, and (2) visual attribute propagation, which transfers attributes between connected entities. Recent advances in low-level vision have been driven by the widespread adoption of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), which rely on grid-structured operations. However, the inherent nature of computer vision tasks involves irregular inputs, making the application of fixed-grid architectures challenging. While some progress has been made using graphs to handle graph-structured data, the majority of graphical convolution methods remain constrained to static graphs that require pre-defined topology. The authors introduce a novel learning framework for constructing dynamic graphs that adaptively models the sparsity and connectivity of graph neural networks. This approach not only captures long-range dependencies effectively but also accommodates the irregularity inherent in computer vision applications. The method's validity is demonstrated through its successful deployment in object detection and semantic segmentation tasks.

Multiplication is frequently employed across numerous applications, particularly in embedded systems where every operation counts. To optimize these multiplications, common techniques such as using only shift and add-subtract operations, implementing recursive hardware structures, or performing approximation are available. This paper presents a novel methodology that simplifies multiplication by eliminating the need for any addition or subtraction operations, only requiring logical shifts and n-nor gates. Multiplers built using only n-nor gates are referred to as "nornors." This study details the design, hardware implementation, and analysis of an 8-bit nornor-based nornor-multiplier.

Quantum deep learning emerged as a promising area with the aim of enhancing the training and deployment of neural networks through the use of quantum algorithms. Although prior research has primarily concentrated on specific network architectures like fully connected layers, there is relatively little understanding regarding the generalization capabilities of quantum models when compared to their classical counterparts. This study presents the first systematic evaluation comparing classical and deep quantum neural networks (QNNs) within the agnostic learning framework. Through analysis of finite-sample error bounds, the authors demonstrate that while QNNs do not offer superior guarantees for approximation tasks from the perspective of sample complexity relative to classical networks, they do provide enhanced guarantees concerning the quantum data density required under certain conditions.

The field of particle physics has witnessed transformative moments in detector technology and data analysis techniques, enabling discoveries across the LHC and its upcoming high-energy physics projects. However, recent innovations in accelerator radio frequency (RF) technology now permit more accurate predictions regarding cavity Q factors and shunt impedances, significantly aiding in the design and upgrade planning for current and future accelerators. This paper examines such advancements and their implications, highlighting updates to key facilities including LHC, ILC, CLIC, and XEN, as well as proposed machines like muon colliders and plasma wakefield systems.

Physicians anticipate discovering new physics at the 100 TeV scale, potentially within the near future. While a proton-proton collider at this energy would offer ample background noise, an $s$-channel lepton collider operating at $\mathcal{O}(100)$ GeV provides exceptionally clean conditions for producing new particles. This paper examines the feasibility of discovering supersymmetry in such a luminous environment. We evaluate how access to long-lived, metastable particles—often obscured in hadron experiments—becomes possible at the lepton machine. Additionally, we analyze production scenarios for supersymmetry via the $Z\tilde{\ell}\tilde{\ell}$ and Higgs-strahlung ($Z\tilde{\nu}\tilde{\nu}$) mechanisms. Our analysis reveals that even with an integrated luminosity of $10~\mathrm{ab}^{-1}$, a 100 PeV collider can discover long-lived sleptons with proper decay lengths of $\mathcal{O}(1\text{--}1000)$ meters extending to masses of $\mathcal{O}(100)$ PeV, and detect sleptons decaying promptly up to masses of $\mathcal{O}(100)$ PeV for the same luminosity.
