We examine the symmetric Tversky ratio models, denoted as $E_\lambda$, which represent orderings, weak orderings, and semi-metrics on finite sets L. It is established that $E_\lambda$ forms a metric if and only if the parameter $\lambda$ equals either 1 or -1; in these specific cases, the model corresponds to the ratio scale models C$_1$ and C-1. Consequently, the collection $\{E_1\}$ union $\{E_{-1}\}$ accounts for every possible application of a ratio scale model C1 or C-1 that serves as a metric over a given finite set K. To address settings involving multiple objects with multiple attributes, we extend these findings by analyzing similar structures across two-dimensional attribute spaces.

Motion deblurring aims to recover sharp imagery from its motion-blurred counterparts. While recent deep learning approaches have achieved remarkable success, these methods typically depend on large synthetic datasets pairing blurred and clear images. The blur patterns in these datasets are constructed using linear operators and physical parameters (such as kernel shape, speed, and direction) defined during generation. Consequently, the quality of this blur ground truth is pivotal for model performance. Existing systems often lack the precision required for practical applications because their linear operators and parameter selections fail to meet real-world standards. This paper introduces a novel data generation framework that significantly enhances the authenticity of blur/blurless image pairs. Our methodology employs a physics-investigated non-linear operator, models complex, nonlinear scanning paths, and utilizes a high-precision camera simulation to craft superior motion blur kernels. The effectiveness of our approach is validated through comprehensive ablation studies and benchmarking against current state-of-the-art techniques on the realistic MotionBlur dataset.

Hebbian learning is a form of synaptic plasticity where neuronal connections are modified based on the simultaneous activation of neurons, enabling adaptive behavior without external feedback. This principle has inspired the design of unsupervised learning algorithms for neural networks, including Resonating Atomic Ensemble (RASE) systems, which have previously demonstrated capabilities such as edge detection and pattern extraction. However, these earlier applications depended on engineered, hard-coded parameters to dictate detection specifics. This paper introduces a software-defined RASE architecture capable of performing general, hard-coded parameter-free pattern extraction. We validate this approach by experimentally confirming the algorithm's ability to learn and distinguish between handwritten and printed characters, a capability that was previously unachieved within the RASE framework.

The ultrapower of any ordered set satisfies the $\eta_{\mathfrak{u}}$-property, where the cardinal characteristic $\mathfrak{u}$ corresponds to the ultrautilized in the construction. This finding offers the first known result using an approach independent of combinatorial set-theoretic methods. It offers an alternative proof for a theorem by J. Paris (1977), which established that every countable ordered set possesses an $\eta_{\omega}$- ultrapower; furthermore, it provides an answer using purely analysis techniques (or theory of ordered structures) without relying on combinatorial arguments.

Scientific research is increasingly characterized by vast datasets, posing significant challenges for data science practitioners. One critical issue is benchmarking multiple machine learning algorithms to determine the most suitable model for a specific task. Although rank aggregation methods are commonly used to synthesize findings from various algorithms, these approaches often overlook the unique characteristics of specific scientific data, which can impact model rankings. We propose a new benchmarking method grounded in Set-valued Reference Taxonomy (SVRT) that explicitly incorporates dataset attributes to predict computational model performance. The SVRT technique involves collecting relevant features for each data set, constructing dataset-specific sets, and calculating the distance between a test set and others within this framework. We integrate several such metrics to assess how well a model is likely to handle a given data set, and then employ rank aggregation to finalize algorithm selection. The researchers tested this SVRT-based approach on a collection of 29 astronomical galaxy datasets, evaluating its efficacy by benchmarking it against conventional methods that benchmark models solely on dataset similarity.

Although it remains unproven, a strong version of a conjecture by Guy Hadwiger suggests that any graph with $k$ in all edges requires at most $k$ distinct colors in its complete coloring scheme. This paper presents novel structural insights into graphs exhibiting high but relatively low minimum coloring requirements relative to what their graph minors would suggest. Our primary structural result reveals that such structures possess either low coloring complexity or contain specific large substructures. More specifically, either the graph is composed primarily of a set of vertices that are mutually adjacent to specific large substructures, or it includes a large structure of a specific type. This approach is applied to verify a strong version of a longstanding conjecture by P. Dirac, which asserts that any graph with minimum vertex degree $k$ must include one of two specific major substructures or a complete subgraph of order $k+1$.

This paper introduces a robust adaptive algorithm utilizing generalized correlation kernels for the smooth recovery of graph signals. The algorithm's kernel width is automatically determined through a least mean squares (LMS) approach. The convergence properties of this system are theoretically examined and subsequently verified by simulation. The ultimate goal of this work is the correction of graph signal distortions, such as those observed in topological defect analysis. We propose an application of this algorithm to reconstruct defects within the brain connectome, comparing simulated outcomes against empirical data acquired from functional magnetic resonance imaging. The results demonstrate that our proposed method achieves a higher degree of smoothing compared to traditional mean curving.

We propose a strategy for generating technical noise-free atomic matter-wave interferometry using optical lattice clocks, a method applicable to other lattice-based systems as well. This approach relies on creating specific classes of atomic entangled states that are then interferenced through the lattice. Our analysis indicates that, when noise is taken into account, both the noise-reduced squeezed states discussed in Ref.\ [1] and our proposed spin-squeezed states perform comparably.

This paper addresses determination problems concerning the anisotropic $p$-LAPLACE and $p$-NEWLTON-COTES operators under the Robin boundary condition. We define the associated energy functionals, derive the variational formulation, and establish the existence of solutions. Our primary objectives are twofold: obtaining sharp upper and lower bounds for the first eigenvalue, and analyzing the minimization of $p$-means derived from these bounds.

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCN) are highly effective for solving problems defined on graph structures. In these networks, convolution layers facilitate the integration of information from neighboring nodes. Although the implementation of this process varies across different libraries and approaches, there is currently no definitive standard. This paper presents a unified mathematical definition for graph convolution operations. We demonstrate implementation examples using popular tools such as PyTorch Geometric, NetworkX, and CUDA with CUDAGRAV. Furthermore, the proposed formula is applied to model molecular properties, showing results in the PMNet model that are comparable to those of state-of-the-art methodologies.

Neural dependency parsing has achieved state-of-the-art performance; however, acquiring substantial quantities of labeled data remains a significant challenge. To address this limitation, we propose an active learning strategy that employs weak labels to refine model training through the selection and treatment of high-confidence samples. Our approach includes a confidence score designed to identify such samples and a specific loss function to effectively penalize errors made on them. We further propose a novel method to generate reliable confidence metrics using a bidirectional Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) structure that synthesizes forward and backward parsing scores. This proposal is presented in two variants: a discrete version operating at the dependency level and a continuous version applicable to raw linguistic inputs. Experiments conducted on English, German, and Swedish demonstrate that our model consistently surpasses baseline approaches, yielding improvements of up to 1.3 Igbert points on English data and similar gains or better on German and Swedish.

This paper examines the transition form factors $f_+(q^2)$, $f_0(q^2)$, and $f_0(q^2)$ governing the exclusive semileptonic decays of $B \to D$, $F$, and $B_s$ mesons into corresponding $D$, $D^*$, and $D_s^*$ states, utilizing the theoretical framework of QCD sum rules. We specifically analyze how the masses of the final-state heavy ($D$, $D_s$, or $D_s'$) and bottom quark sources ($b_q$) influence these form factors. Our theoretical results are contrasted with existing experimental data and lattice QCD computations to assess their precision.

We establish the existence of non-invertible symmetries in $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills (SYM) theories on $\mathbb{R}^{3,1}$ with respect to their magnetic duals. These symmetries generalize abelian global symmetries through fusion with topological defects, specifically zero-dimensional and one-dimensional operators. Analyzing these higher-form symmetries allows us to determine the most general form of the duality, yielding refined versions that apply even when the theories possess no global symmetries.

The Cai-F\"{u}j\'{i}-Immerman query, hereafter referred to as the CFI-query, functions within boolean terms much like a universal quantifier. Its definition relies on a structure known as a G\"{a}bler tree, which branches into constituent substructures called G\"{a}bler components. For any specific class of graphs, the query's universality extends across its G\"{a}bler components, rendering the entire class CPT-definable if and only if that class excludes the G\"{a}bler tree associated with it. Consequently, the computational complexity of model checking for a graph class is governed by the complexity of the problem relative to a class defined as all G\"{a}bler components. This relationship holds true regardless of the structural constraints imposed on the class, assuming the problem remains NP-complete.

Eu2Ir2O7 serves as a prototypical chiral spin liquid, a state characterized by a gapless, entangled network of fractionalized spins that arises from strong magnetic frustration and significant hybridization between Eu$^{2+}$ 4f and Ir 5d orbitals. This study investigates the effects of replacing Eu with isoelectronic Bi at the Eu site within this framework. Our findings reveal a novel Bi-induced gap formation in the frustrated magnetic state of Eu2-xBixIr2O7. We provide evidence that this gap originates from a Bi-driven structural distortion, specifically a reduction in the Bi-O-Bi bond angle, which enhances the Kondo-like coupling between the local 4f/5d moments and conduction electrons. This interaction facilitates a finite density of states at the Fermi level, resulting in a gapped, Kondo-screened ground state. Furthermore, we observe an angle-gapped phenomenon in specific heat and magnetization as a function of the Bi-O-Bi bond angle, underscoring the critical role of geometry in controlling the low-energy physics of these 4f/5d hybridized systems.

Consider a metric space $X$ and another space $Y$ consisting of non-empty compact subsets equipped with the Hausdorff metric. The paper investigates the existence of Lipschitz selections for the mapping $F: X \to Y$, which serves as a set-valued extension of a given function $f: X \to Y$. Specifically, we establish sufficient conditions under which a selection exists that minimizes the Lipschitz constant, provided the function distance from $f$ to the set of all Lipschitz maps is sufficiently small relative to certain geometric characteristics of the domain $X$.

Given $n$-tuples of random variables, we examine their distributional properties conditional on the tuples being both correlated and sum-free. A tuple $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ is defined as sum-free if no subset of its elements sums to another present in the tuple. Our primary focus is on the scenario where each $(i,j)$ pair among $n$ variables shares a fixed correlation $\rho \in (-1/3,1)$. The central result of our analysis demonstrates that the limit distribution, as $n$ approaches infinity, belongs to the class of infinitely divisible distributions. Furthermore, its Laplace transform adheres to an algebraic functional equation. The distribution is characterized by a deterministic measure $\mu$ on the complex plane, where $\mu$ is supported on the interval $[0,1]$. When the correlation is $\rho=0$, the limiting distribution is explicitly $\mu=|\mathbb{P}[Z\in[0,1]]|^2$ for $Z\sim\text{Exp}(1)$.

This paper investigates the effects of run-time configuration specialization on software systems. Gaining insight into this area is crucial for comprehending the broader phenomenon of software specialization and the emerging field of binary-level specialism. The study focuses on Jython configurations, a variant of Jython that enables the Java abstraction mechanism to be bypassed. By adjusting Jython's runtime settings, various forms of specialization were achieved. The study measured non-functional attributes including binary size, resource consumption, and performance. Findings indicate that binary size can be reduced by as much as 90% and performance improved up to 22 times, alongside reductions in memory usage. The paper presents a method for binary size optimization through runtime configuration tuning, a capability not available in previous specializations like Noguist or Shu, and introduces an approach to predict performance based on binary size.

Sub-GeV dark matter represents a compelling candidate alongside traditional, more massive particles, yet its direct detection is fraught with experimental hurdles. Our proposal seeks to overcome these challenges by employing a liquid scintillator loaded with gaseous xenon as the detector medium. Our analysis demonstrates that, to achieve the projected sensitivity of 0.1 GeV/c, the detector requires a size of 0.1 kt. Our study confirms that this configuration effectively suppresses the dominant background noise through the low-pulse height cut inherent to gas xenon's ability to function as a scintillator liquid, thereby enabling robust discrimination against unwanted signals while maintaining high recoil energy sensitivity.

This paper outlines a method for producing the most general class of two-qubit entangled states using two two-level atoms that initially interact via a classical electromagnetic field while individually coupled to an anharmonically coupled-modeless cavity in the anti-Rabi configuration. By employing the Darwin-Lamb shift and virtual transitions induced by the anti-Roci interaction, the desired atom-atom correlated states are assembled within the two-level atoms. Additionally, the article examines how environmental dissipation influences this cavity-mediated atom-atom entanglement.

Accurately monitoring electrocardiogram (ECG) signals is vital for maintaining cardiovascular health, as variations in heart rate (HRV) serve as a critical indicator predicting potential heart conditions. However, existing methods for extracting HRV often struggle with accuracy amidst noise, limiting their practical application. This study introduces a novel deep learning framework designed to streamline HRV estimation by bypassing conventional signal preprocessing and feature extraction stages. Instead, the methodology utilizes an autoencoder to learn HRV features directly from raw ECG data. Our proposed architecture consists of two primary autoencoders: one trained to represent variability characteristics from denoise ECG signals, the other from raw, noisy inputs. Following this, a 1-D convolutional neural network (CNN) analyzes the encoded outputs of both models to generate the final HRV estimation. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, yielding superior accuracy when evaluated against the MIT-BIH ST segment and Arrhythmia Database (MIT-PTDB).

The proposed dataset, HUMBI, focuses on capturing diverse and realistic human bodily icons by synthesizing 3D avatars from single-view inputs through the joint refinement of geometry and appearance. HUMBI integrates diverse methodologies, including neural head/avatar inversion, multi-object detection, and 3D object generation. Our study demonstrates modeling capabilities for five key bodily signals: 3D pose, skeleton, hair, clothes, and faces. To achieve this, we integrate multiple technical approaches: neural inverse rendering is used to model geometry and appearance, while classical computer vision techniques handle the extraction of faces and heads. Additionally, we employ a multi-view 3D generator to model geometry related to hair and clothes, accompanied by a novel detection strategy to locate objects across the multi-view data. Evaluations on SynTH and a novel dataset, HumBlasto—created specifically for HUMBI—highlight the model's superior performance against existing state-of-the-art systems. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ImperialVision/HUMBI.

Although natural language processing languages models have reached remarkable success primarily in English, applications in English之外的 languages remain limited. We introduce a flexible framework designed to transfer English natural language models by leveraging a knowledge graph that maps various task types. This system allows users only to define the structure of their target task within the graph to enable the model's adaptation. We have fleshed out this graph with a collection of natural language understanding and generation tasks, along with corresponding training datasets. We show that existing approaches for model cross-lingual transfer are only a subset capable of being handled by our system. We further compare various strategies for selecting pre-trained models contributed by graph nodes for the purpose of training new models, as well as explore new methods for fine-tuning. The results indicate that our approach performs favorably against state-of-the-art baselines for the tasks we have covered.

This study introduces a novel deep learning framework for temporal video super-resolution (VSR) that leverages flow-guided deformable alignment along with second-order grid propagation to enhance structural details. Specifically, the proposed Second-Order Grid Propagation (SGP) method utilizes accurate optical flow estimates from lower-resolution inputs to propagate grid structures from higher-resolution reference frames upward, simultaneously considering residual errors and temporal gradients; this process significantly improves the recovery of moving objects compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, the Deformable Align-based module (DA-RRA, likely referring to the flow-based alignment mechanism) accurately registers high-fidelity reference frames onto target locations via aligned features, allowing the generation of superior high-resolution guidance for all frames, including those involving motion. As a result, the model achieves significant performance gains, exceeding the state-of-the-art by 0.5 dB (PSNR) on the NTU and 0.4 dB (PSNR) on the COCO datasets, all while maintaining real-time inference speeds.

In the realm of reinforcement learning, related tasks are often trained concurrently using a multi-task approach to benefit from their shared characteristics. However, the inclusion of even a singular, highly divergent task can severely degrade performance on all associated related tasks. This phenomenon arises because standard multi-agent methods typically employ task-agnostic neural architectures, causing the agent to overfit to the features of the easiest or most dominant related tasks while neglect others. To address this challenge, we introduce "Share-Adapt-Rotate," a novel neural architecture designed for learning dynamics-based related tasks. The proposed method achieves robust performance by either rotating the perception or control inputs received from the training environment or by explicitly sharing and selectively adapting the neural representations across different tasks. Empirical results indicate that this approach effectively prevents negative transfer, providing significant benefits even when training on the most strongly contrasting, dissimilar tasks.

We investigate finite-time stochastic heat engines operating between a hot and cold reservoir, focusing on three distinct classes of constraints: (i) fixed bath temperatures scaled by a cycle duration, (ii) fixed cycle duration with bath temperatures scaled by heat exchanged, and (iii) fixed cycle duration with both heat and temperature scaling. For each class, we derive the most efficient protocols, identify the optimal cycle characteristics, and confirm that all allow for analytical solutions. The results are illustrated using the Brownian heat engine model. Furthermore, we compare these findings to determine which scenario yields the highest performance. Finally, we analyze and compare the first law efficiency and the Chernoff information of each engine class as the cycle approaches infinite cycling.

This study investigates the impact of the storm surge generated by the 2005 Hurricane Katrina on the U.S. electricity grid, utilizing a physics-informed machine learning (FML) approach to enhance traditional statistical forecasting. The surge dynamics are simulated with the COHERENT model, while data-driven predictions are made using a convolutional neural network trained on model outputs to capture the intricate, nonlinear relationships between hurricane parameters and surge levels. The convolutional neural network is subsequently integrated with a statistical Generalized Additive Model to construct the convolutional general additive model. The findings demonstrate that this hybrid method effectively improves the prediction of storm surge and significantly outperforms the statistical baseline. By efficiently combining data-driven insights with physical knowledge, this methodology offers a robust framework applicable to other physics-informed data mining challenges.

This text offers a complete analytical formulation of higgs production via single associated jets using perturbative QCD up to next-to-leading order (NLO). The computation integrates virtual corrections with various virtual-real conversion topologies and higgs-emitting parton splitting processes. After expressing these components using color-ordered amplitudes in a color-striped format, the result is summed over color configurations. Numerical validation compares our findings against leading-order simulations and previous NLO calculations, demonstrating excellent agreement.

This study introduces a pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural network designed for efficient and high-fidelity automatic audio synthesis. Our proposed architecture, named PitchEnhanced WaveNet (PitchENet), models the probabilistic distribution of audio wavefunctions, enabling precise and rapid generation of waveforms through sampling. Specifically targeting computational constraints, the network dynamically adjusts its processing based on the detected pitch of a target sound; lower pitches, characterized by longer periods, utilize a smaller network with higher dilation rates, whereas higher pitches engage a larger configuration. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach outperforms the standard WaveNet in both generation speed and quality, achieving Mean Opinion Score scores approximately 0.02 higher at one-fifth the generation latency.

Collaborative Filtering (CF) stands as one of the most popular approaches for generating item recommendations within information filtering systems. However, its efficacy is constrained by the cold start problem, sparsity, and inherent biases. To address these challenges, numerous hybrid models integrating content-based methods with CF have been developed. This study introduces a unified framework that consolidates the core elements found in existing hybrid hybridizations to systematically analyze their effects on recommendation performance. Implemented using the MovieLens datasets, framework evaluations covered three key aspects: (1) a sensitivity analysis examining how user count, sparsity levels, and dataset biases influence results; (2 a correlation investigation into how the strength of content-based components affects CF and overall performance; and (3 a review of strategies to mitigate content-based model biases. Findings indicate a direct relationship where a stronger content-based component improves CF outcomes, yet initial system performance is dictated by CF's ability to overcome the limitations previously outlined.

Doppler techniques face significant hurdles when searching for Earth-like planets due to the masking effect of stellar activity. This research investigates how these activity-induced signals influence the ability to detect potential Earth analogues, utilizing both synthetic spectra and activity indicators to model these variations. By comparing outcomes from inject-and-recover tests, we determine that while indicators offer detection capabilities in specific scenarios, they generally underperform relative to analyses of synthetic radial velocity spectra. The study concludes that incorporating three-dimensional MHD simulations into radial velocity fitting provides a detailed method for assessing and mitigating the impact of stellar activity on detecting planets similar to Earth.

Tunneling between a non-interacting, disordered 2D electron system and a Majorana mode is analyzed in the presence of a magnetic field. For the first time, the evolution of the Majorana peak in tunneling conductance is analyzed as functions of the chemical potential, temperature, and the system's wave function statistics. The study reveals that the statistics of wave functions play the most critical role in determining this peak's behavior. Specifically, for both delocalized and localized states, the peak shifts to lower energies as temperature decreases; however, for localized systems, this shift accelerates significantly in the low-temperature regime. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the tunneling density of states can be made strictly positive by adjusting the chemical potential.

This process additionally leads to a unified definition for what constitutes higher-dimensional right and left homological quadrangle, alongside those adjoined with the relevant structures. As part of this, there is the creation of the "higher-dimensional right and left homological octagon," which functions as an enhanced, triangularly-invariant variant of both previously mentioned quadrangle types when equipped with those respective structures.

While recent Neural Synthesis techniques have shown promise in addressing these issues, they are constrained by the need for large sets of paired image data that is rarely available for general editing. This paper introduces Perceptually-Paired GAN (P2GAN), which utilizes operational-based generative adversarial networks to produce infinite collections of realistic label pairs from a single reference image, effectively making image editing ill-posed problems tractable. This study investigates the settling behavior of snow particles within atmospheric turbulence by utilizing high-resolution numerical simulations of two-phase flows. The study reveals that vortices play a critical role in the dynamics of snow settling. The study shows that the settling process is highly non-uniform in time and space, with the non-uniformity being significantly amplified by vortex structures. The study finds that snow particles are frequently trapped within these vortices for extended periods. The study concludes that these vortex structures act as the primary controllers of the settling process, causing a pronounced non-linear response to changes in particle size.

Active inference is a unifying theoretical framework that addresses the problems of active perception, the integration of information across scales, hierarchical organization, and biological homeostasis. It operates on the premise that biological agents reduce the surprise they encounter by acting in accordance with their own generative models of the world. This text provides an overview of active inference and its unification of homeostasis and cognitive processes within a single agentic theory, highlighting homeostatic mechanisms in the second person. It concludes by exploring active inference's capacity to resolve various complex challenges, unifying these processes under a coherent perspective of surprise minimization.

Gathering data in real-time presents a significant challenge in science, particularly within high-energy physics and cosmology, where the sheer volume of information often exceeds storage capabilities and must therefore be compressed using customized, domain-expert-driven techniques. Conversely, the increasing necessity for flexible, rapid prototyping of machine learning-based compressors complicates this landscape. To address this shift, we present DASH—a decentralized, asynchronous pipeline designed for data handling in large-scale scientific environments. Our implementation showcases a flexible compressor that adapts to specific characteristics of gathering and collection processes while performing anomaly detection to ensure quality control.

This study applies Finzi's novel gravity theory—which predicts enhanced attractive forces at cosmic scales—to the thermodynamics of gravity-dominated large-scale structures. The model posits that the deviation from Newtonian behavior stems from the nonlocal nature of the gravitational potential, and here it is used to derive modifications in the growth of matter fluctuations, the expansion history, and the thermodynamic equations of the universe. Specifically, the first-order corrections (in terms of the small parameter characterizing the long-range enhancement) to the matter power spectrum and background expansion rate are calculated, along with the corresponding adjustments to the matter and radiation energy densities and their associated temperatures.

A subset collection of geometric segments is defined as being $s$-spaced if the Euclidean distance between any distinct pair of points remains at least $s$; the interval threshold for such configurations is denoted by the spacing number $\text{Sp}(2,\mathcal{H})$, which represents the largest integer s-1 where s-1 is not satisfied. The object $\text{Sp}(2,\mathcal{H})$ itself describes the spacing limit in a given convex geometric hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$ on $n$ elements arranged along the perimeter of an $n$-gon, where each edge corresponds to either the straight line segment or a specific curve connecting components of that edge within the partition. While the authors characterize this parameter for specific topological structures, their analysis also establishes sharp upper bounds applicable to general constructions.

Robust climbing robots are essential for applications spanning exploration and search-and-rescue to agriculture. While nature showcases climbing abilities ranging from tiny insects to massive mammals, current artificial robots are often limited by a lack of size and weight diversity. This study introduces Trident, the first artificial system capable of climbing both flat surfaces and inclinations, achieving this through the integration of three key design features: an elastically deformable spine, undulatory body motion, and adjustable limb placement. By simulating the locomotion of Oreina  lucens (a climbing insect), Trident successfully replicated its climbing pattern on level ground and steep angles while executing vertical moves reaching up to 1.25 of its own length. Furthermore, when comparing Trident to existing flat-surface climbing robots, an extensive analysis of undulatory parameters was conducted to determine optimal configurations.

This study introduces a stochastic framework to examine the effectiveness of chemotherapy in combating cancer, modeled as the interaction between two populations: cancer cells and chemotherapeutic drugs delivered at a fixed concentration. The mathematical foundation consists of the Fokker-Planck equation coupled with a hyperbatic transport equation for drug concentration, where stochastic noise arises specifically from fluctuations in the drug's absorption rate within the efficacy model. Key outcomes include deriving the steady states and their stability conditions, as well as establishing the unique existence solution for the model's primary equations. The analysis concludes with dynamical simulations that validate the theoretical findings.

In 1966, Moffatt introduced the concept of topological stretching and twisting for vorticity within inviscid fluids. This paper demonstrates that the corresponding notion of topological area—relevant to both deformable and invincible membranes and established by Elay and the present author in 2002 and 2003—is inherently linked to vortex magnitude. Specifically, during a sequence of deformations where the boundary of a membrane boundary maintains a constant shape while its area remains unaltered, the resulting stretching of an internal region is limited if the initial configuration avoids certain critical configurations. Conversely, if the initial state involves these critical configurations, unlimited stretching potential emerges.

Building on the work presented in \cite{KlSjSt15}, this paper broadens the findings regarding complex geometric optics solutions for d-bar equations in an exterior domain with arbitrary (non-necessarily smooth) boundary. This generalization enables a link between the reflection coefficient and complex geometric optics solutions, thereby establishing a valid complex geometric optics-based scattering theory for data sets derived from a scalar or vector acoustic exterior Dirac problem, provided the sound speed variations satisfy specific decay rates. Furthermore, these results facilitate the creation of such a theory for the electromagnetic scalar external Dirac problem, provided the magnetic permeability variations also satisfy corresponding decay conditions.

We investigate the influence of gravitational radiation reaction on the time evolution of the eccentricities and semi-analytic in-spirals for high-precision, low-frequency systems. Our analysis, grounded in 1st post-Newtonian (PN) theory and applicable to the generic case of non-spinning bodies with arbitrary mass ratios, reveals that the radiation reaction forces the eccentricities of such systems to decrease over time. We demonstrate that the inspiral process drives the eccentricity to a stable "terminal" value at any given Post-Newtonian (PN) order; notably, this terminal value is orders of magnitude larger than what is observed in the field of natural astrophysical systems. Furthermore, we derive the specific functional dependencies of this terminal eccentricity on the dimensionless mass ratio across PN orders, extending our framework to include spinning bodies. These Post-Newtonian results are then applied to a numerical-relativity framework, which enables the extrapolation of these expressions into the strong-field regime. The Post-Newtonian formulas are shown to align well with numerical simulations in the "intermediate" regime—where the Post-Newtonian expansion remains valid but relativistic effects are significant—before we extrapolate the predictions all the way to the final merger phase. The implications of this behavior for future gravitational-wave detection strategies and the parameters of coalescing systems are briefly discussed.

The x-ray free-electron laser (FEL) has become an essential resource for scientific research, and the chirped undulator technique is known for substantially enhancing its efficiency and boosting lasing power. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the interaction between lasing radiation and electrons within the chirped undulator environment, examining the effects on spectral brightness, saturation characteristics, and the overall gain. We also examine how the introduction of transverse modulation influences these outcomes. Furthermore, we extend the standard 1-D analytical one-particle model by incorporating a 2-particle approach to explicitly address particle interactions. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings through numerical simulations using a 3-particle interaction model.

Event detection is a critical component of real-time decision-making in graph analysis, yet graph structures often undergo continuous changes that make identifying events a challenging task. Existing methods typically struggle with the evolving nature of these graphs, frequently overlooking key issues such as lack of interpretability and poor generalization. To address these shortcomings, we introduce Discrete-time self-supervised event detection using Dynamic Graph Contrastive learning (EDGC). This framework dynamically aligns representations of consecutive temporal snapshots to derive detection features, while the contrastive loss enhances feature discrimination. Furthermore, we employ a discrete-time self-supervised objective during training that emulates self-supervised labeling, enabling model application without the need for ground-truth events in the testing or deployment phases. Evaluations across three real-world datasets confirm that EDGC achieves competitive performance, delivering both high accuracy and reliable outcomes.

This work examines the resolution of the Euler equations for an ideal gas featuring a free boundary, where we enforce a pressure of zero across this limit to capture the state beyond the gas. We analyze the case where a strong shock wave accelerates, approaching a regime where the non-zero shock velocity renders the Mach number close to unity. We demonstrate that as M approaches unity, the shock wave's dynamics can be accurately approximated by a model consisting of a system of three ordinary differential equations. This result extends earlier research by Majda [J. Amer. Math. Soc., 3 (1990), 895-920], which derived a similar reduction for an accelerating contact discontinuity in a polytropic gas, and aligns with investigations by [J. Diff. Eq. 123 (1996), 103-133] regarding shock oscillations in a stratified gas. We further apply this simplified framework to predict specific characteristics of the flow field in the immediate vicinity of the shock front.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has progressed significantly over the last decade, with a critical focus shifting toward the explainability of these increasingly sophisticated models. As AI applications permeate critical domains such as healthcare, law, and transportation, there is an urgent need for frameworks that can effectively communicate complex decision-making processes to non-technical stakeholders. This study introduces "Copilot," an interactive web application designed to satisfy varying explanations requirements across diverse stakeholder groups. By integrating a multi-agent architecture grounded in Distributed Decision Making (DDM), Copilot functions as both a collaborative interface facilitating interaction between users and decision systems, and a DDM tool facilitating inquiry into an system's internal logic. We outline the application's design principles, present initial use-cases, and discuss strategic directions for future development.

Characterizing colorectal polyps through histopathology is essential for determining personalized surveillance intervals and preventing cancer. To support pathologists, deep neural networks have been developed to assist in supporting them. However, existing methods often rely on synthetic annotations, which are derived from coarse labels found in colorectal cancer datasets. This study introduces an innovative approach that creates annotations specifically for the synthetic histopathology by utilizing expert-derived descriptions. Based on these synthetic annotations, we generate models for predicting both the organ of origin and histological features. Although designed to augment clinical tools, this work also advances understanding of current limitations in synthetic annotation methods.

This work addresses a guessing scheme where an adversary attempts to guess the output of a stochastic channel driven by a secret source. The source encoder's objective is to minimize the adversary's success probability while ensuring the adversary can recover the original secret source with probability exceeding a specified threshold. This formulation is equivalent to optimal source coding under source-side uncertainty regarding the channel. We establish that the worst-case maximum $q$-entropy leakage is bounded by $\left[ D_q^{\varepsilon}(\mathcal{V}\| \mathcal{U}) \right] \cdot D_q^{\varepsilon}(\mathcal{V}\| \mathcal{U})$, where $\mathcal{V}$ and $\mathcal{U}$ represent the stochastic source and channel, respectively, combined with the source coding rate $D_q^{\varepsilon}$. To address scenarios involving the simultaneous decoding of multiple correlated stochastic sources by the adversary, where a specific subset must be successfully recovered, we extend this framework. Our main result shows that the maximum $q$-entropy leakage is at most the sum of the $\varepsilon$-Rényi divergence for each individual stochastic source plus the $D_q^{\varepsilon}$ term.

Deep generative models are highly effective for imaging reconstruction from severely undersampled data. We introduce a new approach that formulates generative model-based compressed sensing as an optimisation task, aiming to identify the specific latent vector within a pre-trained generative model that yields the sparsest code relative to a sparse dictionary. We Owing to the non-convex and challenging nature of this specific optimization problem, we developed the "Sparse Latent Optimization" (SLO) algorithm. This framework is notably versatile, supporting various non-sparse constraints and regularisers. We have also designed a specific dictionary learning protocol to pre-compute sparse representations for the learned latent values. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses traditional reconstruction methods, including other data-driven techniques.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) stands as a leading candidate for executing near-term quantum computers to tackle combinatorial optimization problems. Although existing research primarily utilizes hybrid QAOA implementations that depend on classical feedback for parameter tuning—a constraint that may limit its effectiveness as classical resources become scarce—this paper introduces a fully quantum version capable of this hybrid-free parameter estimation. The study evaluates the efficacy of the standalone quantum algorithm using two distinct quantum ansätze, specifically the $C_{\beta}$ only and $\gamma,\beta$ circuits, across various multivariate polynomial functions. This allows us to determine multivariate polynomials capable of approximating key hybrid QAOA metrics, such as the expected fitness value, within those hybrid frameworks. The findings demonstrate that for a given qubit and layer count, free-parameter selection via the hybrid method generally yields superior outcomes compared to using fixed parameters. Furthermore, the results indicate a lack of definitive proof supporting any single class of multivariate polynomials as universally adequate for predicting hybrid QAOA fitness expectations.

This paper introduces **EllipticGS**, an open-source Python library designed to compute geometric metrics for ellipses. We begin by outlining fundamental geometric properties—such as segment areas and distances from centers to nearest and furthest points on the ellipse boundary—that are derived from elliptic integrals. The work then details the specific algorithms implemented in the library, which include calculations for these metrics as well as the shortest path (geodesic) between any two points on the ellipse.

Because analytical solutions for elliptic integrals generally do not exist, we evaluated the practicality of numerical methods versus high-precision approximations. The analysis reveals that for most geometric purposes related to ellipses, approximations outperform pure numerical calculations due to their superior speed, with no measurable loss in accuracy. The paper concludes by providing a comprehensive comparison of these approaches and verifying the libary's functions against previously published results found to be consistent. EllipticGSGS is accessible at https://github.com/jeffreyhs/EllipticGS.

This work introduces a continuous-time reinforcement learning framework grounded in the quasi-isometric function (q-function), a temporal extension of the discrete-time value function. For a specified policy, the q-function corresponds to the expected cumulative discounted reward, where future rewards are evaluated using an exponential decay factor tied to the squared elapsed time rather than the number of steps, with no discount applied at t=0. We define the instantaneous advantage flow as the difference between the q-function and the action-value function for any given behavior policy, from which the policy gradient for that policy can be directly derived. A key contribution of this framework is demonstrating that the optimal policy maximizes the expected instantaneous advantage rate, allowing for the formulation of a novel policy gradient estimator. We further examine on-policy learning algorithms capable of approximating both the q-function and optimal policy parameters, demonstrating these methods in a linear quadratic regulator task using both simulated environments and real robotic hardware. Results indicate that the proposed learning approach in the robotic setting performs comparably to, and in certain aspects surpasses, existing state-of-the-art methodologies.

Our model incorporates the Hubbard repulsion alongside effective magnetic exchange interactions that include both nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor components with opposite signs. Within this extended framework, we develop a hybrid numerical strategy combining Kogut-Suthland's method with a tailored self-consistent iteration process to solve the resulting non-linear equations. This allows for the calculation of the complete spectrum of magnetic modes across the Brillouin zone for various ground states. We find that due to the sign disparity in magnetic exchange interactions, the system exhibits a non-linear Kato anomaly, yielding an accidental zero mode at the $\Gamma$ point. Precise vertebral localization and identification (VLII) are essential for numerous clinical applications, yet they remain difficult due to anatomical challenges such as the pelvic bone, sacrum, and the varying vertebral body sizes and shapes. Furthermore, pathologies like degenerative disc disease, vertebral compression, and deformities including scoliosis and kyphosis exacerbate the difficulty. While recent deep learning methods have made significant strides, they often lack robustness against these specific issues. This paper introduces a novel deep learning framework for 2D VLII designed to handle pathologies and challenging body regions effectively. The method employs coordinate-based embeddings to represent vertebral shapes and uses patch-based localizations to determine spine boundaries. During both training and inference, a multi-scale strategy is applied to mitigate distortions caused by body shape variations. The proposed approach was evaluated on two datasets: one collected from emergency room patients at a US hospital covering 10,532 chest X-rays, and another synthesized with augmented pathological features on normal scans, consisting of 20,932 abdominal images. Experimental results indicate superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

Stochastic Thermodynamics models thermodynamic systems as random walks influenced by time-varying control parameters. In the framework of Mean Field Theory, a key advancement is understanding the system's behavior through the scaled cumulant-generating function (SCGF), which offers profound insights into long-time dynamics, particularly regarding fluctuations. This work establishes a general gauge invariance within Stochastic Thermodynamics, demonstrating that an specific relationship must hold between the driving protocols and the SCGF when these vary slowly. Consequently, this finding allows for the classification of distinct thermodynamic regimes based on expansion orders of the SCGF regarding time-scale separation. We apply this expansion to a Landau–Zener transition, illustrating how it yields meaningful predictions regarding higher-order stochastic variations.

This study investigates the wave scattering occurring in two parallel piezoelectric semi-infinite solids, which share a common interface and are positioned within a medium capable of transmitting electro-magnetic waves. By utilizing fundamental solutions for elastic, electric potential, and magnetic field fields, the authors derive closed-form expressions for an associated boundary value problem. The analysis begins with an overview of the fundamental solutions required, followed by the formulation of a system of boundary value problems based on specific physical constraints applied to in-plane transverse wave excitations. The subsequent section presents an analytical method for resolving these specific value problems. The final section examines various energy transmission scenarios involving incident in-plane and transverse waves, highlighting the roles of electric and magnetic interactions in these processes. The study concludes that electromagnetic wave theory supports complete blocking of both in-plane and transverse waves in piezoelectric materials when the wave is polarized along the propagation direction; however, full blocking does not generally occur for waves polarized perpendicular to the propagation direction.

Experiments have demonstrated that excitonic reservoirs regulate the many-body interactions of polariton condensates, influencing their characteristics. In this study, we examine how spatial features of a nonresonantly pumped background determine reservoir distribution using a microcavity containing a semiconductor crystal of defined geometry. The experiment involved a 50 µm diameter GaAs cylinder, excited by a Gaussian beam with a 3 µm spot size. Our measurements revealed a significant disparity between the room-temperature carrier spatial profile and that of the polariton density; specifically, carriers accumulate at the cavity edges due to strong exciton-exciton interactions within the condensate. This observation supports theoretical modeling based on short-range interaction assumptions and suggests an experimental approach to spatially engineer reservoir distribution by cavity shape, potentially enabling the creation of various polariton states with tailored properties.

The disintegration of exoplanets serves as a dynamic process that offers valuable insights into the environment causing their destruction. Specifically, the rate of erosion provides a measurement of the host star's XUV flux, while the chemical composition of the remaining planet yields information about its internal structure. This paper outlines the physical mechanisms driving atmospheric stripping and explores how observations can be leveraged to understand both the planetary interior and the local stellar environment.

I argue that it is counterproductive to evaluate Galileo's legacy as the pioneer of modern, experimentally driven science given his relatively limited hands-on experience with experiments. Instead, I propose viewing his mathematical rigor and logical deduction—tools that are timeless—as the true foundation from which scientific experimentation grew. This perspective suggests his emphasis on mathematics stemmed not only from training but also from the availability of powerful mathematical methods capable of producing significant physical insights. I further contend that had effective experimental methods existed during his time, Galileo likely would have adopted them. This essay seeks to expand the criteria by which Galileo is judged, shifting focus away from his mathematical preferences and toward the broader methodological framework he employed.

The generalized thermodynamic attributes of a system are defined by the grand potential, with its associated equations of state derived through differentiation. This framework is particularly valuable for analyzing the ionization of hydrogen and helium within astrophysical environments, such as the interstellar medium and the solar wind, where we calculate the pressure required to sustain a specific volume at a given temperature and chemical potential. Our investigation reveals that, unlike the case for pure gases, the presence of a chemical mixture causes the ionization boundaries to shift. This modified ionization front correlates with the grand potential and exhibits greater steepness compared to the boundaries predicted by the Saha equation. Consequently, the transitions appear more abrupt when observed in the context of the grand potential.

Collisionless magnetic reconnection is a central focus in space and astrophysical plasma physics, where it is typically analyzed using kinetic models. However, simulating these systems with a fully self-consistent kinetic approach is currently restricted by computational cost to the reconnection diffusion region alone. To study the broader system, we must simulate the interaction between this central zone and the surrounding magnetized outflow, a task that demands hybrid techniques. These methods must engage the outflow kinetically while treating the diffusion region with physics-based initial conditions or numerically. In this work, we examine the interaction of an outflow with a pre-existing magnetic field using a novel kinetic simulation initialized via the Parker-Glaststone model. By doing so, we bypass the need to resolve the complex microphysics within the diffusion region numerically, instead seeding the outflow plume with specific ion distributions derived from kinetic theory. Simulation results indicate that, comparable to fully self-consistent runs, the outflow interacts with the ambient field to form a de-Haénes layer and exhibits bursty Hall resistance. These findings demonstrate the efficacy of initializing plumes with Parker-Glaststone distributions and offer valuable insights for applying this methodology to reconnection events in solar and stellar coronas, as well as in accretion flows.

Problem-solving chatbots engage users in interactive challenges aimed at boosting their cognitive abilities. Unlike passive systems typical of natural language dialog (NLD), these chatbots demand user initiative and strategic thinking within the conversation. Effective implementation requires not only the capacity to initiate and manage a problem-solving scenario but also the ability to interpret the underlying objectives when analyzing unstructured input. This paper introduces a novel discourse analysis approach specifically designed for problem-solving chatbots. The methodology employs a two-step process: (1) identifying the speaker active in the dialogue and (2) locating a speaker attribution label from a predefined set within the conversation history. We evaluate the approach using both deterministic rule-based strategies and machine learning models, achieving accuracy scores of 90.5% (rule-based) and 96.1% (ML). These results surpass previous state-of-the-art methods by 3.1 percentage points and exceed the baseline by 5.6%.
